World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018782/Hainan to Ban Sales of Gas-Powered Vehicles From 2030
World.title: Hainan to Ban Sales of Gas-Powered Vehicles From 2030
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018782/Hainan to Ban Sales of Gas-Powered Vehicles From 2030
World.content:
China’s southern island province of Hainan will become the country’s first to ban the sale of gasoline-powered vehicles by 2030, domestic media reported this week.

A plan released by the provincial government on July 3 requires that all new vehicles in both the private and public sectors — including buses, taxis, and rental vehicles — be EVs by 2030, with the exception of “special purpose” vehicles. The province also aims to maintain a ratio of one charging pile for every 2.5 EVs.

Existing gasoline-powered vehicles will still be allowed on the road after the ban takes effect, and hybrid vehicles will continue to be sold. The province will also increase the share of new energy vehicles on its roads to almost half, up from under a quarter in 2025.

The province, known for its beaches and resorts, first proposed banning the sale of gasoline-powered vehicles by 2030 in 2019 and has since issued a series of policies outlining a roadmap toward that goal.

The province has also consistently led China in EV adoption. This April, EVs accounted for nearly three-quarters of all new vehicle sales in Hainan, the highest share nationwide.

Experts told domestic media that Hainan’s geographic advantages as a small island have helped accelerate the transition. Many of China’s latest EV models can complete the province’s popular 600-kilometer coastal highway on a single charge, while its warm climate largely mitigates cold-weather battery performance issues.

Gasoline in Hainan has long cost more than 1 yuan ($0.14) per liter above prices in most other provinces, Zhang Xiang, an auto industry analyst, told domestic media.

Since 1994, Hainan has bundled road maintenance fees and tolls into a fuel surcharge, making it the only province in China without highway toll stations.

While the surcharge encouraged the shift toward EVs, the shrinking number of gasoline-powered vehicles has also decreased road maintenance funds. To address this challenge, Hainan last year proposed a system — yet to be implemented — that would charge drivers based on vehicle mileage.

With the maturation of China’s EV industry in recent years, vehicle reliability and driving range have improved significantly. The share of EVs among new vehicle sales nationwide rose from under 6% in 2020 to over half in 2025. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in 2019 that it would support pilot programs to phase out gasoline-powered vehicles in regions “with suitable conditions.”

EV-driven reductions in oil consumption have become a key driver of cleaner air in China, according to a report released by the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) on July 14.

The report estimates that EVs displaced 33.7 million tonnes of oil equivalent in the first half of 2026, roughly equal to 6% of China’s crude oil imports in 2025.

“That said, those gains could quickly taper off as China’s PM2.5 improvement curve flattens, meaning further progress will depend on more of these kinds of structural changes: cutting coal-related emissions on one side and reducing petrol and diesel combustion on the other,” Qi Qin, a China analyst at CREA, said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018778/China’s Scenic Spots Chase Views. Travelers Want the Real Ones.
World.title: China’s Scenic Spots Chase Views. Travelers Want the Real Ones.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018778/China’s Scenic Spots Chase Views. Travelers Want the Real Ones.
World.content:
In the end, it wasn’t the crowds that made Xiao Minhan lose her appreciation for China’s tourist sites — it was a blue-and-white street sign. On it, where you’d expect to find the name of a street, was written: “I’m in Chongqing, missing you.”



The signs began appearing in the southwestern megacity in 2022, which is when Xiao, a 32-year-old travel enthusiast from Beijing, encountered her first. “At the time, I thought it was a bit artsy and distinctive, so I took a photo and posted it on WeChat Moments,” she tells Sixth Tone, referencing the Chinese super app’s social post feature.



But soon, she found that identical signs had popped up at nearly every scenic spot she visited around the country, with only the place name swapped out for those of other cities and villages — even the names of cafés, stores, and events.



“Seeing it over and over again, I don’t feel like taking photos anymore — (the signs) just make the place feel tacky,” she says. “Domestic tourist attractions are becoming increasingly homogenized.”

Dummy street signs were just the beginning. China’s tourist sites now increasingly feature cheap, garish objects like plastic flowers and oversized plush toys crammed into natural landscapes and on centuries-old temple eaves. Rustic towns by day have become neon nightmares by night. Million-year-old stalactites drenched in rainbow lights have been reduced to gaudy karaoke sets.

Chinese travelers are noticing the tacky trend — and they’re not happy. In April, netizens slammed a cheap, plastic, multicolored heart sculpture amid the salt lakes and snow-capped mountains of the country’s northwestern Qinghai province as an “eyesore.”

The scenic area responded that they had had it professionally designed because they believed some visitors wanted more photo spots to “check in,” or daka, a phenomenon in which tourists mark where they’ve been by taking and posting photos of themselves at a location.

But travelers were not appeased. The heart sculpture set off a wave of online backlash toward tasteless tourist spots, with a top comment on WeChat reading, “Our Eastern aesthetics are almost disappearing in front of these cookie-cutter influencer-style tourist spots. It’s really disrespectful to the aesthetics of our ancestors.” In a popular comment on microblogging platform Weibo, one user also asked, “Can’t our scenic spots leave nature untouched?” The topic has since accumulated over 26 million views.

A China Youth Daily survey of 1,334 people in June found that almost 85% of respondents considered aesthetic quality important when choosing a destination. Moreover, 95% reported encountering “aesthetic disappointments,” with more than one-fifth saying they see them “frequently.” Most respondents blamed over-commercialization, as well as the pursuit of money and viral trends, for the trend.

In response, from May 15 to June 5, lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, launched the “Scenic Area Aesthetics Revival Plan,” inviting users to post beautiful sights captured during their trips. The related topic has been viewed over 77 million times, with some posts garnering over 20,000 likes.

Now, attractions are also shifting away from their past “tacky” aesthetics to simpler decor, in line with tourists’ wishes.

Cultural empathy



Xiao is equally disheartened by the growing uniformity of China’s “ancient towns,” often once historical, densely populated areas that have been given a facelift. She says that towns even thousands of kilometers apart share astonishing similarities — shops along stone-paved streets selling the same souvenirs, and the air always smelling of stinky tofu, despite the snack originating in eastern China.



“I try to avoid these so-called ‘ancient towns’ when I travel in China now,” Xiao says. “They all feel like copies of the same theme park.”



Zhang Yujia, a Gen-Z traveler from Shanghai, echoes this sentiment. Recalling Huishan Ancient Town in the eastern city of Wuxi, she said that man-made additions spoiled the views. The paths were lined with historic buildings, yet cheap red-and-yellow paper lanterns hung from trees along the street, disrupting the town’s overall black-and-white architectural style. “There isn’t a single photo-worthy spot,” she says.

For Min Guan, founder of the Beijing-based rural revitalization consultancy Future Rural Lab, the problem stems from the effects of social media. “The rise of social media has turned travel photos into social currency, fundamentally shifting tourist motivations from ‘I want to go’ to ‘I want to be seen,’” he says.

He argues that “check-in” culture should serve merely as a small component of a destination rather than its main draw.

“The problem with homogeneity is that it’s easily replicated and quickly fades,” Min says. “There are no winners in the ‘check-in’ business model: the market is cutthroat … tourists end up having poor experiences, and local culture loses the ‘soil’ it needs to grow.”

Lin Bishu, a professor at Xiamen University’s School of Management, traces the problem to a loss of culture. “Unique local histories, dialects, folklore, and architecture are stamped out because communities lack the means of telling their own stories,” Lin says. “Instead, they rely on generic internet templates, slogans, and viral symbols to replace cultural expression.”

Lin says “check-in” culture can rapidly boost visibility at a low cost, especially for niche destinations, but the long-term damage is significant. “When travel devolves into mere photography, tourists lose the opportunity for deep cultural experiences and empathy,” he says. “Once the photo is taken, disenchantment sets in.”

To preserve cultural idiosyncrasies, Lin advocates establishing strict standards to define core local symbols and values. Protecting indigenous residents, traditions, and ways of life is crucial, allowing culture to grow organically rather than artificially, he says.

He points to Preikestolen, or Pulpit Rock, in Norway​ as a prime example of sustainable tourism. The site preserves the original cliffs and natural landscape, all without commercial development or the viral gimmicks he sees at many “check-in” sites in China. “It embodies a philosophy of respecting nature, prioritizing preservation over development, and maintaining authenticity, which could be a model for China’s natural heritage sites,” Lin says.



To avoid tacky tourism, some Chinese scenic spots are already taking a different approach: doing less.

The Xixia Imperial Tombs are one such example. Located at the foot of the Helan Mountains in northwestern China, the site holds the burial grounds of emperors from the Western Xia dynasty (1038–1227).

Here, there are no fake ancient streets, no plastic flower walls, no ugly swings. Signage and railings blend into the landscape, preserving the raw, windswept feel of the thousand-year-old tombs.

Since becoming a UNESCO site in 2025, the tombs have drawn growing crowds. Earlier this year, the site’s stone guardians, deliberately designed to look broken, went viral on Chinese social media. Visitors praised the site, with one highly upvoted comment reading, “The damaged statues, set against the vast northwestern landscape, have become the site’s most poetic feature.”



Tianzhang Temple in the eastern Zhejiang province also recently went viral for its unique Song-dynasty (960–1279) aesthetic of space and restraint — a lawn, a stone path, and a few understated Song-style buildings — with netizens lauding it as “the pinnacle of Chinese-style aesthetics.”

As for Zhang, her favorite destination is Wuxi’s Li Garden. “In spring, standing on the opposite bank, I saw willow branches and peach blossoms blending like an ink-wash painting,” she recalls.

“I’d expected it to be just an ordinary park, but it turned out to be far more stunning than I ever imagined.”

Additional reporting: Mao Rui; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A woman poses for a photo amid plastic flowers decorating a waterfall at a scenic spot in Luoyang, Henan province, 2025. Image from Xiaohongshu)

World.title: From Chaoshan, Into the Stars
World.content:
This is the fourth article in a series on China's southern Chaoshan region, exploring the history, culture, and identities behind its recent resurgence in the spotlight. Read Part 1, Part 2, and Part 3.

Thousands of light-years away, on a planet illuminated by a binary star system, humans have built a city that floats on the tides. An intelligent system governs the sleep, diet, and travel of everyone living there. Yet when a group of the planet’s inhabitants — descendants of people from Chaoshan, a region in southern China’s Guangdong province — hear the drumbeats of the Yingge dance, they feel the same passionate physical response as did their distant ancestors.

This is the basic premise of my recently published young adult sci-fi series, the “Raging Yingge” trilogy. In it, I wanted to convey an idea that I’ve become increasingly convinced by in recent years: Chaoshan people may well be among the first humans willing to migrate to the stars — but they would also bring their customs with them.

Over the past few centuries, this coastal region has been the origin of one of the world’s largest Chinese diasporas, with millions of people of Chaoshan heritage now living across the globe. From Southeast Asia, Europe, and North America, they run businesses everywhere from Bangkok’s Chinatown to Paris’ 13th arrondissement. Wherever they go, they still speak the Chaoshan dialect, eat beef meatballs and noodles, and worship the same deities and ancestors.

I myself am a native of Chaoshan. I grew up in Shantou, Guangdong province, near the historical district of Xiaogongyuan, where there was a Bo Gong temple by the entrance to the alley. Bo Gong is the local earth deity, and almost every neighborhood has a temple dedicated to him. Locals passing by drop in to pay their respects or cast divination blocks to ask their fortune, just like people nowadays pull out their smartphones to ask artificial intelligence. I can still remember the smell in the temple: incense ash mingled with the fishy scent of the wet market that clung to my nostrils and refused to fade. Some people prayed there, others cried, but most just nodded as they passed. A single temple bound together the beliefs and destinies of thousands of households across the neighborhood.

Back then, all I could think about was escape. At school we were taught materialism, while at home I was irritated by the endless rounds of ancestral rites and holiday rituals. I fought with my grandmother over the television remote: She wanted to watch Chao opera, while I wanted cartoons. When I left for university in Beijing at the age of 18, I felt a wave of relief as the train pulled out of the Chaoshan plain. At last, I was leaving behind this small, old place with all its rules and conventions.

However, after turning 30, my perspective completely reversed. While at Google, I’d have meetings with French, Thai, and American colleagues, and when I asked about their ancestry, it turned out they all traced it back to Chaoshan. Later, when I went to Shenzhen, I’d hear the Chaoshan dialect as I walked along the street and see beef hotpot restaurants everywhere. It was only then that I realized that Chaoshan people had already been practicing decentralization for generations. From stepping aboard the pioneering, iconic red-head junks and sailing to Nanyang in the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), to the network of Chaoshan merchants scattered around the world today, wherever they settled, they remained recognizably themselves.

Gradually, I came to understand what holds this whole web together. It isn’t scripture, doctrine, or political power — it is a web of human relationships. The nodes are ancestral halls, the connections are kinship ties, and the protocol is an unwritten ledger of favors and obligations passed on by word of mouth. This system was lightweight enough to fit into the hold of a red-head junk bound for a new world, yet resilient enough to operate simultaneously in the rice paddies of Siam, the rubber plantations of Malaya, and the streets of Paris. What’s more, the polytheistic and animistic nature of Chaoshan faith means that each Bo Gong temple has served as a self-contained node wherever it was moved and rebuilt. In modern-day terms, this was a distributed cultural-survival framework.

Meanwhile, qiaopi — remittance letters exchanged between Chinese migrants overseas and the families they left behind — play an important role in this framework. A single qiaopi doesn’t look like much, yet it serves as the trust protocol of this distributed network. As long as one letter is sent and another is received, two people on opposite sides of the ocean can be simultaneously present in each other’s reality. Chaoshan people call this “carrying someone in your thoughts.” People are not afraid of poverty, distance, or death. What they fear is the severing of these ties.

So when I say that Chaoshan people are suited for interstellar migration, it’s not just a joke. The hardest part of settling a new planet has never been rocket thrust: It’s whether a social system can be transplanted. A bureaucratic apparatus is too heavy to bring along, and there’ll be no one to enforce a constitution. Bring a clan network instead, then the ancestral hall becomes the community center, the ledger of favors and obligations becomes a mutual-support network, and the Bo Gong temple becomes a spiritual anchor. It doesn’t rely on any external infrastructure because it’s composed of those countless ties of gratitude, grievance, and longing that bind people together.

This points to a fundamental difference between the rooted, yet mobile Chaoshan approach toward embarking on voyages and the frontier Western narrative of exploration. In the classic image of interstellar exploration presented in Anglo-American science fiction, a person stands on the surface of a strange planet, looks back at their spaceship, and then heads out into the wilderness. He is saying goodbye to his old world. But this is not how Chaoshan people go out. When the red-head junks left Zhanglin Port, no one truly looked back. It’s not because they weren’t reluctant to leave, but because everything was already on board the ship: ancestral tablets, soil from their hometown, and agreements recording who had contributed money and labor. They weren’t leaving Chaoshan at all. They simply rolled it up, slung it over their shoulders, and carried it with them, spreading it to more distant and unfamiliar seas and countries. They never truly left.

Of course, this cultural tenacity has another side, and Chaoshan contains a structural contradiction, one that has taken me many years to understand. On the one hand, there is a deeply conservative insularity: family, ancestral halls, dialect, offerings — all that must be protected, passed down to the next generation, and not altered. On the other hand, there is an intense drive outward, borne by the geography itself — going out to sea, doing business, leaving for foreign countries, and expanding business to every corner of the world with a port. The two forces operate simultaneously within the same group of people — and I’m no exception. Rather than go into business as many had assumed, I insisted on writing science fiction. Rather than having men perform the Yingge dance in line with Chaoshan traditions, I deliberately made a young girl the lead dancer in my novel. Every Spring Festival, a kind of gravitational pull deep inside my bones draws me back to Shantou. But once I get home, all those rituals and conventions make me uneasy. To call it reconciliation would be too simple — it’s more like an endless tug-of-war.

And yet, this very tug-of-war is what creates both tension and momentum. Looking inward preserves the cultural core, while reaching outward prevents it from turning into a fossil. Twisted together, these two forces have allowed Chaoshan people to endure the currents of globalization longer than most communities. The same is true in writing. The most interesting things often emerge from the space between these two forces.

I’ve coined a term of my own for writing that explores this: “Chaoshan futurism.” In it, you throw a highly local culture into a far-distant future shaped by algorithms and interstellar distances and then watch what happens when the two collide. In a city where AI controls everything, who will people perform the Yingge dance for? Who will the kung fu tea be brewed for? And will there still be deities to answer the prayers offered in a Bo Gong temple?

While writing my trilogy, I came to understand that these concrete, everyday acts are why the Chaoshan people haven’t disintegrated despite being scattered around the world for several hundred years. These seemingly insignificant acts are the smallest units of cultural survival. They don’t require anyone’s approval or an institution’s support. As long as people continue to exist — and as long as human ties and affections remain — they will continue to survive. And what’s more, they’ll likely last much longer than we can even imagine.

It’s now 2026. AI is writing poems, creating art, and making decisions for us. But there is one problem that algorithms cannot solve: They don’t know what it means to carry someone in your thoughts. No large language model can calculate how a migrant bound for Nanyang might compress all the complexity of longing, worry, and affection into a few brief lines for family members across the sea. The amount of computation contained in that moment exceeds anything humanity has ever encoded into an algorithm, because it isn’t the optimal solution — it’s the most human one.

Translator: David Ball.

World.title: All-Women ‘Shaolin Soccer’ Tribute Scores Big, Divides Fans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018769/All-Women ‘Shaolin Soccer’ Tribute Scores Big, Divides Fans
World.content:
Renowned Hong Kong actor-filmmaker Stephen Chow’s new kung fu football comedy, “Kung Fu Soccer,” has generated a wave of nostalgia in China and grossed over 660 million yuan ($100 million) at the box office in just four days.

Released Saturday, the film is the best-attended and highest-grossing summer film debut in China in the last five years. Chow’s first film in seven years is considered a tribute to his 2001 comedy “Shaolin Soccer” and follows the Emei women’s football team, a modest group named after the famous wuxia martial arts sect. The players employ classic kung fu moves, often flying through the air to beat their rivals.

The film attracted significant investment. According to ticketing platform Maoyan, it was backed by 18 production companies and six co-producers, with a reported total investment of 380 million yuan.

Renowned for his signature mo lei tau, or “illogical,” comedy style, featuring exaggerated performances, absurd elements, underdog stories, and unpredictable twists that often satirize social conventions, Chow is widely regarded as having played a defining role in the development of on-screen Chinese comedy.

Unlike Chow’s previous football film, which centers around an all-male team, “Kung Fu Soccer” features female protagonists. It also explores how its characters reconcile with winning and losing, rather than how ordinary people rise to prominence through hard work, as was often the focus in Chow’s earlier films.

Prior to the release of “Kung Fu Soccer,” anticipation was high on social media. Many reposted the phrase “I owe Stephen Chow a movie ticket,” an apologetic reference to the prevalence of piracy of Chow’s past films in the Chinese mainland.

However, after watching the film, many reneged on their promise, posting instead that it was not viewers who owed Chow tickets, but rather the director who owed them tickets — in part because they were let down by the comedy.

Many complained that the film’s jokes felt outdated, with exaggerated performances, abrupt character development, and disjointed transitions between plot points that reminded some of “short-video compilations.” Others criticized the film for its jarring and distracting visual effects, including glowing football fields and players transforming into tigers, leopards, and dragons mid-match.

And without Chow himself performing his signature mo lei tau comedy, as he has previously done, many said the actors’ attempts to imitate his style come across as awkward and failed to capture its essence.

Beyond its comedic shortcomings, some viewers also critiqued the film for sexism. On multiple occasions, female players use sexually suggestive moves to distract the male referees, while one of the Emei footballer’s special skills is triggered after seeing her toxic ex-boyfriend kissing another woman.

As of Tuesday, the film holds a score of 6.6 out of 10 on Chinese review platform Douban. In a highly upvoted comment, one user wrote, “Chow’s fascination with social outsiders is still present in the film, as is his fondness for eccentric characters. The film sometimes even offers glimpses of the magic that once defined his work.”

“The problem is that these moments are all too brief. Just as they begin to rekindle your expectations, they are quickly interrupted by an outdated meme, an over-the-top performance, or an overly sentimental scene,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Kung Fu Soccer.” From Douban)

World.title: France star Kylian Mbappe breaks FIFA World Cup career goal record
World.content:
SCORER. France's Kylian Mbappe reacts after their bronze-medal match against England in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

France's Kylian Mbappe ends the 2026 FIFA World Cup with 10 goals, two ahead of Argentina's Lionel Messi in the competition for the Golden Boot

France didn’t get the win but Kylian Mbappe got the record on Saturday, July 18 (Sunday, July 19, Manila time). For now.

The French star became the all-time leading goal scorer in FIFA World Cup history with 22 after two goals in his club’s third-place match against England in Miami Gardens, Florida.

Despite Mbappe’s efforts, France lost 6-4 as its attempted comeback from a 4-0 halftime deficit fell short.

Mbappe scored goals in the 48th and 66th minutes to move one ahead of Argentina great Lionel Messi.

“I’m just trying to help my team score every time,” Mbappe said after the match. “It’s for sure that when you score that many goals in the World Cup, it elevates you to certain levels but I would have liked to not be the top scorer in history and play tomorrow’s (championship) match.”

“So, I think it’s good for legacy and when we stop (playing) to say that I was one of those players. But today, it’s not the first thing crossing my mind.”

Mbappe also has 10 goals in this World Cup, two ahead of Messi in the competition for the Golden Boot. Messi’s squad meets Spain in the final in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on Sunday, meaning the Argentine star has a chance to surpass both marks Mbappe set.

Mbappe is the first player with 10 goals in a World Cup since West Germany’s Gerd Muller in 1970. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Lorna Kapunan, private prosecutor in Sara Duterte impeachment trial?
World.content:
The celebrity lawyer is no stranger to handling high-profile cases and lawyering for controversial public figures

Lorna Kapunan is perhaps the most recognizable name on the list of private lawyers who make up the prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Her first major appearance in the high-stakes affair happened on Tuesday, July 14, when the lawyer manifested the prosecution’s intent to withdraw Office of the Vice President chief of staff Zuleika Lopez from their witness list.

Kapunan is one of the first people enlisted by the House in their team. When the House first impeached Duterte in 2025, Kapunan expressed her desire to participate in what she had described then as the “trial of the century.”

“It is our duty to stand for what is right. It is our duty as lawyers to stand for justice, and we see that this whitewashing, we see that this burying of evidence, we see that this brazen violation of the Constitution, and the principle of accountability is being violated,” Kapunan said in an interview with DZMM at the time.

Play Video

There’s no surprise that Kapunan chose a career in law. After all, she is the daughter of Lino Mejia Patajo, a former Supreme Court associate justice, whom Kapunan fondly remembers as her “anchor and moral compass in life and in law.”

A political science and law graduate from the University of the Philippines, Kapunan began her career as senior associate at ACCRALAW in 1978. She stayed there until 1986, after which she began managing her own firms. Today, it is known as the Kapunan and Castillo Law Offices, which she founded in 2011.

She is the widow of former trial court judge Eduardo Ronen Kapunan, whom she lost to cancer in 2001. Her son died from leukemia two years later, a tragedy that inspired her to co-found a support group for mothers who lost their children.

Kapunan prides herself as a women’s rights advocate, and was even chairperson of the United Nations Development Fund for Women. But she also once drew criticism for representing controversial male clients, such as Dr. Hayden Kho, and Kris Aquino’s ex-husband James Yap.

The celebrity lawyer is no stranger to handling cases that captured national attention. These include:

The West Tower Condominium vs. First Philippine Industrial Corporation (FPIC) case: Kapunan served as counsel for the petitioners who complained about a pipeline causing hazardous leakage. The case is known for triggering the Supreme Court’s first ever writ of Kalikasan.

Pork barrel scam queen Janet Lim Napoles’ serious illegal detention case, which Kapunan withdrew from as lead counsel in 2013 due to “difference in opinion” with another lawyer on Napoles’ team.

A class suit where she represented Philippine Airlines flight stewardesses, who sued the airline for compulsorily retiring them at 55 years old while their male counterparts could retire at 60.

The fatal hazing case of Horacio Castillo III, whose family she represented. A Manila court convicted her for unjust vexation over remarks she made while working on the case.

The missing cockfighters case, in which she briefly lawyered for businessman Charlie “Atong” Ang.

Kapunan also cultivated political ambitions. She ran for senator in 2016 as part of the slate of then-senatorial aspirant Grace Poe, but only placed 29th after receiving over a million votes.

Kapunan’s legal career brought her beyond the courtroom and into the broadcast studio, as she also served as a television host for various shows, such as Aliw23 TV’s “Laban Para sa Karapatan”, DZRJ TV’s “Legally Speaking,” and TV5’s “FACE 2 FACE.”

On Wednesday, July 15, Senator Pia Cayetano called out Kapunan for offering a lengthy explanation on why the prosecution dropped Lopez from the witness list. Some senator-judges claimed such statements could affect the impeachment court’s impartiality.

“When we talk about balance and when we talk about impartiality, that same standard should apply not only to the prosecutors, not only to the defense, but to the senator-judges,” Kapunan later said. – Rappler.com

Isabel Victorino is a fourth year AB Communication student at Ateneo de Manila University and a writer for its school publication The GUIDON. She is currently a Rappler intern.

World.title: Users of Meta’s Facebook, Instagram report suffering some outages
World.content:
FACEBOOK. Facebook app icon is seen on a smartphone in this illustration taken October 27, 2025

Some Facebook and Instagram users experience intermittent access to the two social media platforms

Meta’s Instagram and Facebook social networks appeared to suffer some outages on Sunday, July 19, with users reporting issues with the app and website.

According to website downtime monitoring service Downdetector, there were 4,808 reports filed by Facebook users in the United States as of 0746 GMT, with 63% of users facing issues accessing the website.

Another 2,829 reports were filed by Instagram users in the US who faced issues with the app as of 0818 GMT on Sunday.

Checks by Reuters also found that access to Facebook and Instagram was intermittent in Singapore.

Meta did not immediately reply to a request for comment sent by email. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Why you need to help independent newsrooms
World.content:
Unlike lies — which you can pull out of thin air — ‘the best obtainable version of the truth’ takes time, talent, resources, and courage

We totally get it.

People are so used to getting content for free that it’s hard to imagine why you would need to pay for it. Why shell out money for content when Facebook, Tiktok, and YouTube are teeming with creators who repurpose stories and share their “analysis” of current events for free, at the drop of a hat?

The attention economy is a cutthroat space that newsrooms cannot win now — unless we succumb to ridiculous antics, screaming headlines, and short “analyses” that many content creators of today resort to just to get eyeballs.

The traditional way by which newsrooms earn revenue to support themselves is through advertising. But that model has long gone down the drain. Nearly 80% of global media advertising is now cornered by the top 10 tech companies: Google, Facebook, Amazon, etc. To get to the remaining 20%, newsrooms from all over the world have to fight tooth and nail with each other, with an ever growing number of influencers and content creators, and — more recently — with an avalanche of AI slop.

Yet, most Rappler stories remain free. We are committed to our public mission to deliver verified information on matters of public interest.

Only select Rappler exclusives require a paywall. But we also produce short video derivatives from them to serve for free on TikTok and YouTube. It’s a constant source of joy to see these videos on corruption and geopolitics watched by millions of viewers.

We require people to register (via their emails) — for free — for two reasons: We want to make sure that humans, not bots, are on our site (and even then this has become uphill battle because of the sneaky ways of AI) AI companies steal our content as training data — without seeking permission and without paying. They then deploy information to readers who would otherwise find them in news sites.

For fact checks that Rappler makes, readers are not even required to register.

It is when we publish investigative stories and premium analyses that we ask the public to help us sustain this kind of work by joining our Rappler + membership program. And we appreciate that they do, because this simple act of citizenship inspires us further to tell stories that those in power prefer not to be told.

Rappler + members believe that journalism is vital to making governments and communities work, and they part with their hard-earned money to help ensure that this work continues.

We grant, however, that it’s not a small ask if one takes into account the shrinking personal and household income of Filipinos. That said, we used to pay for newspapers. We also paid for cable news.

As of 2022, the Philippine Statistics Authority even estimated that one in 10 Filipino families are already subscribed to streaming services like Netflix.

Estimates peg the amount Filipinos spend on mobile games at roughly US$1.5 billion.

We also pay for more frivolous things online. Lazada, Shopee, and Temu are flourishing here. Even Amazon has found it lucrative enough to enter the Philippine market.

If you find value in the investigations and in-depth reporting that Rappler has been delivering, surely you will not find the small amount of P247 a month or P3,500 a year prohibitive?

Yet, when we release exclusive, well-researched, original content on disinformation narratives or anything of public interest, we get comments like these: “Galit kayo sa disinformation pero yung information, lalagyan nyo ng paywall.”

As one fellow journalist said, this is how journalism dies: when people think it always needs to be given away for free.

It is as if Rappler does not have to pay for what goes through the process of researching, investigating, editing, publishing, and keeping a workforce. The meter for our hosting server does not stop when the subject matter of an article a user is accessing is a public interest issue.

The inconvenient truth here is this: unlike lies and conjecture — which you can pull out of thin air — ”the best obtainable version of the truth” takes time, talent, and resources. And, yes, courage.

Thus, Rappler and other newsrooms are facing the challenge of coming up with multiple revenue streams to sustain the business — through membership programs and other revenue pillars.

It’s a battle we won’t win without our public.

We ask that you will pass on this message so more people will support independent journalism.

Thank you. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: Democratic Taiwan must not become ‘China’s Taiwan,’ president says
World.content:
LAI CHING-TE. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te speaks at the annual congress of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in Taipei, Taiwan, July 19, 2026.

Lai Ching-te says Taiwan must remain vigilant in times of peace, pointing to China's 'legal warfare,' such as its new ethnic unity law which gives Beijing the basis to take action against people outside its borders

Taiwan must work together to protect its democracy and not become part of China, President Lai Ching-te said on Sunday, July 19, calling on members of his Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) to oppose the “red terror” coming from Beijing.

Lai, who won election two years ago, and his ruling DPP, champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing which views the island as an inviolable part of Chinese territory.

Speaking to the DPP’s annual convention, Lai said Taiwan must remain vigilant in times of peace, pointing to what he said was China’s “legal warfare”, such as its new ethnic unity law which gives Beijing the basis to take action against people outside its borders.

That has alarmed Taiwan, because it could give Beijing another legal basis to try and prosecute or arrest Taiwanese it views as separatists. China has rejected all criticism of the law. China’s legal system has no jurisdiction in Taiwan.

“I also expect comrades within the party to stand on the front lines, unite as one, and jointly oppose the threat posed by China’s ‘red terror’ to Taiwanese society,” Lai added, speaking in Taiwanese, also known as Hokkien or Hoklo, rather than the main language of government, Mandarin.

“We must work together to protect our democratic and free way of life, and absolutely never allow ‘democratic Taiwan’ to turn back and become ‘China’s Taiwan’,” he said.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China has rebuffed Lai’s repeated calls for talks, calling him a “separatist”.

Lai, who is also DPP chairman, reiterated that Taiwan is already an independent country, whose constitutional name is the Republic of China, and it is not subordinate to the People’s Republic of China.

“Regardless of ethnic group, regardless of who came earlier or later, anyone who identifies with Taiwan is a master of the country. Taiwan’s future must be decided jointly by the 23 million people of Taiwan,” he said.

The defeated Republic of China government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists, who formed the People’s Republic.

To this day neither government formally recognizes the other and no peace treaty to end the civil war or armistice has ever been signed.

Over the past decade of DPP government, Lai said Taiwan had not backed down in the face of “authoritarian expansion,” disinformation attacks, military threats, and diplomatic pressure.

“Taiwan has shown the world that democracy is not a weakness; democracy is strength,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: EJ Obiena vaults to best mark since Olympics
World.content:
AIM. Pole vaulter EJ Obiena in action for the Philippines in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand.

Looking like his old self again, Filipino pole vaulter EJ Obiena achieves his highest clearance in nearly two years as he bags silver in Spain

MANILA, Philippines – EJ Obiena is gradually rediscovering his old, dangerous form.

The Filipino pole vaulter set his best mark in nearly two years as he cleared 5.85 meters to bag the silver medal in the Meeting Madrid in Spain on Thursday, July 16 (Friday, July 17, Manila time).

It marked Obiena’s highest clearance since he recorded 5.90m in the 2024 Paris Games, where he finished fourth and fell short of an Olympic bronze by a single attempt.

Germany’s Bo Kanda Lita Baehre struck gold in Madrid with a personal-best 5.90m.

Obiena skipped 5.90m for 5.95m in a bid to supplant Lita Baehre from the top but missed the mark in all of his three attempts.

Portugal’s Pedro Buaro also hurdled 5.85m like Obiena, although he settled for bronze via countback.

Obiena has consistently passed 5.80m as he made the height in his last three meets, clearing 5.81m for fourth place in the Fly Athens in Greece and 5.80m for sixth place in the Gyulai Istvan Memorial in Hungary.

Before that stretch, that last time Obiena leapt past 5.80m was at his home event, the Atletang Ayala World Pole Vault Challenge, in September 2025.

Obiena’s resurgence bodes well for his cause, especially with the Asian Games, which will be hosted by Japan from September 19 to October 4, coming up.

The only Asian member of the six-meter club, Obiena is the defending champion of the quadrennial showdown after ruling the 2022 edition in China. – Rappler.com

World.title: Singer-songwriter ORIGIN builds his own universe through music
World.content:
Based in Hiroshima, Japan, Filipino singer-songwriter ORIGIN hones in on nostalgia and the little things to tell stories in the music he makes

Growing up, Yzlvikxen Angkahan would never be caught without a sketchbook and art materials in hand. Drawing was his favorite hobby, and he made sure everyone else around him knew that.

“I made drawing my personality,” he confessed in a mix of English and Filipino. “‘At school, people would say, ‘That’s Yzl drawing over there.’”

It was what his peers associated him with all the way up until high school. Even when he transitioned to photography in his late teens, things didn’t feel too far off from the Yzl who liked to draw as a kid. He was still a visual creative through and through.

These are the markings of someone who would eventually go on to become an artist in adulthood. It was true for Yzl, but not in the way you’d think.

These days, you won’t find him hunched over a canvas, but behind the mic as singer-songwriter ORIGIN.

One and done? Not quite

Like most (if not all) Filipinos, ORIGIN was a music fan who just liked to sing here and there. He had a microphone at home, but he had still never thought anything of it. As far as he was concerned, music was just something he enjoyed and never took all that seriously.

But things would change when the pandemic hit. He would join Discord servers where people would just sing and play around with vocal effects, and from the confines of his bedroom, he would teach himself audio mixing. Before long, he’d finally gather the courage to sing into the mic.

“The moment I heard myself with effects for the first time, it was like an ‘Oh shit’ moment for me. Kasi parang, ‘Uy, gagi, ang angas pala ng tunog ko ‘pag may effects (Because it’s like, ‘Hey, my voice sounds pretty cool when there are effects),” he told Rappler. “It gave me a boost of confidence.”

ORIGIN. Photo courtesy of the artist

And when he took things a notch further by making his voice heard on those Discord servers he joined, he would soon realize that he could actually sing.

This is where his artist name would come to be, too. It’s a funny story, really, and there isn’t anything deep to it. He needed a Discord username, and remembered that he had just bought a new pair of shoes in the colorway “Origin Story.” Since then, it’s stuck.

Everything would quickly follow from there — including the heartache that would pretty much kickstart his music career; he just didn’t know it yet.

On May 19, 2022, ORIGIN would get his heart broken, and while romantic letdowns are always unfortunate, it had led to him writing his first-ever song, “NINETEEN.” When he wrote it the very next day, he pieced together that not only could he sing, but he could write lyrics pretty well, too.

“I never stopped writing since. I fell in love with songwriting after finishing my first song,” he said.

He released “NINETEEN” in early 2023, and that was supposed to be the end of it. It was all meant to be a one-time thing, where he had just wanted to check releasing a song on Spotify off his bucket list.

But when people actually started streaming it and adding it to their playlists, ORIGIN thought it wouldn’t hurt to drop another song, and then another, and another.

“I was confident about music from the get-go,” he said about finally sharing his work to the public. He had yet to figure out what his sound truly was at this point, but even then, he knew this was his moment, and he wasn’t going to let anyone downplay that.

Even more releases and three years later, ORIGIN has never looked back.

A storyteller

Now based in Hiroshima, Japan, the 27-year-old artist finds joy in creating a sense of nostalgia for those who listen to his music. In his lyrics, he dives deep into the small details of the past. He zeroes in on the little things you likely wouldn’t take notice of in the moment — but only when the memory has long passed.

Reality and fiction blur in his world. ORIGIN is a storyteller who knows how to build a whole new universe around him by taking pieces of real-life moments and letting his imagination do the rest.

Just listen to his song, “Distraction.” Here, ORIGIN goes back to the time when he was talking to someone who suddenly got busy. He was still vying for her attention, but he couldn’t help but feel like he was a distraction to her.

He confessed that not everything he says in this song actually happened in real life. What he does is add color to the otherwise mundane, and perhaps that’s the charm behind his music. He prefers to keep his lyrics simple, and just lets his creativity do the talking.

“I’m not a fan of using flowery words when it comes to writing,” he shared. “How you’d say it in real life, gusto ko gano’n ko rin siya isusulat (I want it to be written that way, too).”

As a human being, though, there’s another interesting quality to ORIGIN. There are light spots that envelope parts of his skin, and while he had desperately tried to cover these up when he first got diagnosed with vitiligo some years back, it turned out to be what helped him gain confidence like no other.

“In ‘EARLY SLEEPER,’ the cover art is showing my whole face. Nung napost ko na siya, parang okay lang naman pala (When I posted it, it turned out to be okay). People actually didn’t care about it,” he recalled.

His skin condition isn’t something he wants to be defined by, but it also isn’t something he’s going to push away.

IN HIS OWN SKIN. Because of his vitiligo, ORIGIN has learned to become confident with who he is. Photo courtesy of the artist

“Siguro kung wala akong vitiligo ngayon, I wouldn’t be as confident,” he told a friend. “I wouldn’t be forced to put more love sa sarili ko. Maybe that’s why I have this.”

(Maybe if I didn’t have vitiligo now, I wouldn’t be as confident. I wouldn’t be forced to put more love on myself. Maybe that’s why I have this.)

Big dreams, even bigger possibilities

Beyond all this, however, one of ORIGIN’s most striking qualities is that he has faith in his own music, and is well aware of the village it took for him to get to where he is now.

He credits his success to his producer, Corrgtd, who he had collaborated with to put together many of the songs on his catalogue — “2021,” “Mirror You,” “Kalamidad” with El Manu, and his latest single, “maliliit na bagay.”

“My producer Carlo Oraya (Corrgtd) has been really helpful with shaping how my music sounds. This guy trusted me since day 1 nung dalawa pa lang songs ko (when I only had two songs) and we just clicked after doing our first song. All of my songs are collaborative work and I’m very hands on with the process. That’s why every song is personal to me,” he said.

ORIGIN can vouch for his own body of work, and isn’t afraid to aim high. He dreams of becoming one of the Philippines’ top songwriters, and while he knows it’s a big dream to fulfill, he still believes that nothing is ever truly impossible.

“This guy never misses when it comes to releasing songs. It’s always catchy. It’s always radio-friendly. That’s the type of stuff I want people to feel,” he told Rappler.

He’s well-aware that there’s a long way to go, but he maintains confidence that his music can reach the people who are meant to hear it. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Argentina is the FIFA World Cup’s favorite villain
World.content:
GREAT. Argentina's Lionel Messi celebrates after Lautaro Martinez scores their second goal in their semifinal against England in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

From Diego Maradona's defiance to Lionel Messi's global celebrity, Argentina has long inspired devotion at home and abroad, alongside irritation, envy, and resentment from rivals

For some fans following this FIFA World Cup, the calculation has been simple: support whoever is playing against Argentina. Across the tournament, that has meant wearing the green of Algeria, the blue of Cape Verde, or the red of Switzerland. Even the often maligned England got a boost in global social media pledges of support last week ahead of their semifinal clash. And in the final on Sunday, July 19 (Monday, July 20, Manila time), it may mean pulling on a red Spain shirt.

Argentina is one of football’s most successful and recognizable national teams, but also one of its most polarizing. From Diego Maradona’s defiance to Lionel Messi’s global celebrity, the Albiceleste have long inspired devotion at home and abroad, alongside irritation, envy, and resentment from rivals.

The Maradona legend

Argentina’s football identity has been shaped by extraordinary individual players of global fame. Maradona provided Argentina with its most defiant sporting myth, leading the country to the 1986 World Cup title. His two goals against England in the quarterfinals — the infamous “Hand of God” and a solo run later voted “Goal of the Century” — remain central to Argentina’s football narrative.

The memory of the “Hand of God” goal still stings for many English fans, while Argentines often view it as part of a larger story of defiance and revenge after the 1982 Falklands War, in which Britain kept control of the disputed island territory.

After Argentina’s 2026 World Cup semifinal win over England, players brandished a banner reading “Las Malvinas Son Argentinas” (“The Falklands are Argentine”), in reference to the long-running dispute over the islands, in apparent contravention of FIFA rules banning political statements.

The Messi effect

Lionel Messi gave Argentina a different kind of icon to Maradona: quieter in public, but with greater global reach and longevity. He won nearly every major honor at club level with Barcelona, becoming the face of a dominant side, though that success made him a target for rival fans.

His rivalry with Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo added another layer, splitting global football into Messi and Ronaldo camps.

After years of being compared to Maradona and nagged for failing to deliver a major tournament title for his country, Messi led Argentina to the 2022 title in Qatar. His continuing presence has made Argentina a magnet for admirers, including in India and Bangladesh, many miles from Argentina. But others have wearied of the Messi-centric narrative and the adulation surrounding him.

A complicated neighbor

Argentina’s image in Latin America is complex. The country has long seen itself as culturally distinct, shaped by strong European influences and a football culture that often treats victory as proof of national exceptionalism. That self-assurance is sometimes admired, but in parts of the region it also feeds a stereotype of Argentine arrogance.

Fans of many nations use tournaments to display national pride with drums, flags and chants, but the fanaticism of Argentina can seem extreme at times.

And that nationalism can veer into uglier territory. One Argentine TV commentator earlier this month called Mexicans “detestable” and accused them of envying Argentines “not just in soccer, in everything,” remarks that Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum called “outrageous.”

In the stadiums, some fans still chant an offensive song that mocks the African origins of many France players, one that Argentine players in 2024 apologized for after singing it. Other incidents involving racism or disorder by Argentine fans have been shared on social media or complained of by other supporters.

Deep rivalries

Argentina’s deepest rivalry is with Brazil, rooted in decades of competition between South America’s two most successful nations. At the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, Argentine supporters chanted, “Brasil, decime que se siente” (Brazil, tell me how it feels), taunting the hosts while reveling in Argentina’s progress.

Tension with Chile intensified after Chile beat Argentina in the 2015 and 2016 Copa America finals, both on penalties. Mexico and Argentina have also developed a charged football relationship, fuelled by repeated World Cup meetings and social media debates over performance.

Argentina’s playing style — defined by virtuosity and cunning — can be joyful to watch but is also seen by some as against ideals of fair play.

For some fans, “anyone but Argentina” has become a default tournament position. – Rappler.com

World.title: No province left behind as House pushes for rural development – Dy
World.content:
House Speaker Faustino `Bojie’ Dy III.

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives is committed to ensuring that every province benefits from national development as it pursues measures to expand opportunities for families, strengthen local communities, and speed up growth nationwide.

According to a statement on Sunday, Dy stressed the point on Saturday in a message delivered on his behalf by Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez during the 60th Foundation Anniversary of South Cotabato and the 27th T’nalak Festival.

In that message, he noted that South Cotabato has shown over the past six decades what could be accomplished when government and citizens work together.

Article continues after this 

READ: World Bank to fund P45-billion rural program – Marcos

“Every great community is woven together by people who choose unity over division; who choose service over self-interest; and who believe that our diversity is our greatest strength,” Dy said.

“Progress is never woven by one person. It is woven by an entire community. And weaving that future is not finished in a celebration,” Dy said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Drawing inspiration from the T’nalak Festival, he likened the province’s colorful handwoven fabric to the collective effort required to build stronger communities despite differences in culture and tradition.

Dy also highlighted several education and nutrition measures approved by the House before the close of the First Regular Session of the 20th Congress, including the expansion of the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE) Program, the strengthening of the Last Mile Schools Program, and the proposed National Nutrition Program, which seeks to expand school-based feeding and other nutrition interventions for Filipino children.

Article continues after this 

READ: DA sets over P600-M rural infra projects in E. Visayas

“Laws matter. But what matters even more is whether people actually feel the difference. Because the true measure of every law is not what is written on paper. It is what changes in people’s lives,” he said.

Article continues after this 

As Congress prepares to open its Second Regular Session, Dy said the House remained focused on passing legislation that responds to the real needs of Filipinos.

“We continued to listen to the voice of our local governments and our citizens to make sure that every law that we pass responds to your true needs and the challenges that your communities face,” he said.

Dy also stressed the House’s commitment to equitable national development, particularly for communities outside Metro Manila.

World.title: Laoag PWDs, advocates unite for fun run to champion disability rights
World.content:
PROMOTING INCLUSIVITY. Persons with disabilities (PWDs) receive special prizes during the 2026 Lakad/Takbo sa Komunidad Tungo sa Pagkakaisa, held along Gilbert Bridge in Laoag City, Ilocos Norte, on July 19, 2026. It event aimed to foster inclusivity and encourage community engagement, particularly among PWDs and their families. (Photo by Leilanie Adriano)

LAOGA CITY — Hundreds of persons with disabilities (PWDs), their families, advocates and government agencies gathered here on Sunday for a fun run and walk to promote inclusivity and physical fitness in celebration of National Disability Rights Week.

Richard Ramos Jr., president of the Laoag City Federation of PWDs, said the Lakad/Takbo sa Komunidad Tungo sa Pagkakaisa highlights the importance of creating inclusive communities where PWDs can actively participate in sports, education, employment, and other aspects of public life without discrimination.

“We are here to show that there is unity and inclusivity among us,” he said, citing that proceeds raised from the registration fees of around 600 participants will fund activities to promote the rights and welfare of PWDs.

Article continues after this 

The federation has over 3,000 active members in this city.

Kristoffer Raymund Medina, officer-in-charge of the Persons with Disability Affairs Office (PDAO), said that through events like these, PWDs feel empowered because they are seen and supported by the government.

The city government’s PDAO continues to offer various programs and services for PWDs.

Among these are the provision of assistive devices such as wheelchairs and walking aids; hygiene kits and food packs, as well as free cinema access and a social pension for eligible beneficiaries.

Organizers, in partnership with PDAO, said this is the second time they have hosted the event with the support of public and private sponsors.

Article continues after this 

Mary Ann Jacinto, a mother of 14-year-old wheelchair user Angelyn from Barangay Cavit, expressed her joy over her daughter’s participation in the event.

“I am glad that we have an opportunity like this to celebrate diversity, foster social inclusion, and advocate for the continued promotion of disability rights,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Jacinto hopes more activities such as the fun walk and run will inspire greater understanding, acceptance, and respect for PWDs.

On June 19, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. declared July 17-23 as National Disability Rights Week through Proclamation 597, affirming the country’s commitment to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disability. /apl

World.title: PNP to deploy over 20,000 cops for Marcos’ 5th Sona
World.content:
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. (Photo from PNP / Facebook)

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Sunday said over 20,000 personnel will be deployed to ensure the peaceful and orderly conduct of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth state of the nation address (Sona) on July 27, 2026.

According to the PNP in a statement, a total of 20,229 law enforcers will be deployed to implement its comprehensive security preparations.

READ: PNP: Final readiness checks underway for Marcos’ fifth Sona

Article continues after this 

“The deployment reflects the PNP’s dual objective of securing the Sona while ensuring that police services remain uninterrupted in communities across Metro Manila,” the PNP said.

Among the deployment, 5,904 personnel have been designated to sustain anti-criminality and other police operations, ensuring continuous police visibility, crime prevention, and emergency response even as security measures for the Sona are intensified.

Meanwhile, 2,345 personnel have been assigned to the House of Representatives, which will serve as the main venue of the president’s address.

Additional personnel, on the other hand, will be positioned in designated staging areas, major thoroughfares, transport hubs, checkpoints, emergency response units, public assistance stations, as well as other key convergence areas.

This is to maintain public order, facilitate traffic management, and provide immediate assistance before, during, and after the event.

Article continues after this 

PNP chief PGen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said that the organization is fully prepared to carry out its mandate with professionalism, discipline and respect for rights.

“This is not just about the security of the Sona. What is important is that police services continue to be provided to our communities as we ensure that this event is held peacefully and in an orderly manner,” he noted.

Article continues after this 

“We want every Filipino to feel safe—whether they are attending the event, going to work, or simply carrying on with their daily lives,” he added. /apl

World.title: VP Duterte’s bank, tax docs best defense vs unexplained wealth claims – Tolosa
World.content:
Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr., House prosecution panel spokesman and private prosecutor — Screengrab from INQUIRER.net video

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte should let her lawyers present her bank and tax records before the Senate impeachment court, as they would be her defense against the accusation that she had amassed unexplained wealth.

Lawyer Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr., House prosecution spokesperson and private prosecutor, made that proposal on Sunday in an interview over AM radio DZBB’s “Bantay Balita sa Kongreso.”

Those records, Tolosa pointed out, would best counter the findings of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) that she had misrepresented her wealth in her statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ridon: Subpoena for VP Duterte financial records backed by Constitution

“So if they really want to prove that the amounts in their bank records or account in this period were not that big, shouldn’t they themselves show their bank records?” Tolosa said in Filipino.

He also pointed out that the prosecution was not seeking a general inquiry into all of Duterte’s bank accounts. Rather, it was merely asking the Senate impeachment court to subpoena specific accounts already identified in AMLC reports, complete with the corresponding account numbers and branch information.

Suspicious transactions

Tolosa recalled that, during the clarificatory hearings of the House committee on justice, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified that reports reflected P6.7 billion in covered and suspicious transactions involving the bank accounts of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, from 2005 to 2026.

In response, the vice president’s camp claimed that the amount was inflated because it could have included repeated deposits and withdrawals or transfers between Duterte’s own bank accounts.

Article continues after this 

Tolosa argued, however, that those explanations made disclosing the actual bank records even more important.

“Now, those are what will give proof of what the bank accounts really contained in the same period,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Tolosa stressed the prosecution’s position that Duterte did not fully disclose her assets in her SALNs, considering the billions of pesos disparity between the transactions reported by the AMLC and Duterte’s declared net worth of P88.5 million in 2024.

READ: VP Duterte’s financial activity surged in public office – Diokno

To determine whether she had unexplained wealth, he said the impeachment court must compare the assets declared in her SALNs with her income tax returns filed with the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), the AMLC reports, and the balances reflected in her bank records.

Only by examining these documents together, he said, can the impeachment court determine whether Duterte’s total wealth was substantially greater than what she declared while in public office.

The continued opposition of the defense to releasing the records raises more questions than it answers, Tolosa said.

World.title: Ridon: If ‘Mary Grace Piattos’ does not exist, who got the money?
World.content:
Rep. Terry Ridon —File photo by Grig C. Montegrande | INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The identities of “Mary Grace Piattos,” “Milky Secuya,” and other individuals listed as the supposed recipients of confidential funds from the Office of the Vice President will be among the key issues when the House prosecution begins presenting evidence on the impeachment article accusing Vice President Sara Duterte of misusing P612.5 million in confidential funds and committing a betrayal of public trust.

Rep. Terry L. Ridon made that statement during the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City.

The defense, he added, should explain who actually received confidential funds if the supposed recipients would turn out to be fictitious.

Article continues after this 

READ: Let NBI chief testify on VP Duterte’s threats vs Marcos – Ridon

“We will talk about Mary Grace Piattos [at the trial]. Who is Mary Grace Piattos, and is Mary Grace Piattos a real person?” Ridon said in Filipino.

“If Mary Grace Piattos is not a real person, then who got the money for which Mary Grace Piattos signed?” he added.

Alleged misuse of OVP confidential funds

The prosecution is scheduled to begin presenting evidence on the confidential funds charge on July 22.

It has already completed its presentation on the impeachment article involving Duterte’s alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez.

Article continues after this 

The impeachment article accuses Duterte of misusing a total of P612.5 million in confidential funds — P125 million spent by the OVP in the final 11 days of 2022, P375 million in OVP confidential funds in 2023, and P112.5 million in confidential funds spent by the Department of Education in 2023 while she was concurrently its secretary.

Ridon said the prosecution would present records from the Philippine Statistics Authority showing that no birth, marriage, or death records could be found for Piattos, Milky Secuya, and several other names listed as recipients of confidential funds released by the OVP.

Article continues after this 

“We will talk about the PSA report that nobody was born, died, or was married named Mary Grace Piattos, Milky Secuya, and other names in the list of recipients of confidential funds of [the OVP],” he said.

READ: NBI chief will be last witness in VP Duterte threat issue July 21

He said the prosecution would also call a National Bureau of Investigation handwriting expert to testify on similarities among signatures appearing on acknowledgment receipts bearing different recipients’ names.

The prosecution also plans to present the findings of the Commission on Audit, including the notice of disallowance covering P73.287 million in confidential expenses incurred by the OVP in 2022.

Ridon said the disallowance had already become final at the level of the Commission on Audit Proper.

World.title: Zamboanga del Sur provincial gov’t refutes P1.6B COA scrutiny claim
World.content:
INQUIRER.net files

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — The provincial government of Zamboanga del Sur has denied reports online that the province is under intense scrutiny over a supposed P1.6-billion Commission on Audit (COA) finding.

It branded the report as “highly misleading, malicious and defamatory.”

Atty. Jose Ruel Saniel, Provincial legal officer, said in a statement on Sunday that the allegations spreading on social media and select media outlets are “completely false, baseless and stripped of proper administrative context.”

Article continues after this 

He noted the narrative “was deliberately crafted to erode public trust in a provincial leadership that has consistently upheld transparency and good governance.”

Saniel clarified that the provincial government has systematically addressed all Audit Observation Memorandums (AOMs) raised by state auditors.

“We have submitted the necessary legal justifications, reconciliations, and supporting documentation,” he said.

“In cases where certain items were disallowed or disapproved, the province accepted the findings and committed to discontinue such practices, strictly following COA’s recommended formats and processes,” he noted.

He emphasized that proactive compliance ensures every peso allocated for Zamboanga del Sur’s development is accounted for and utilized, in accordance with government procurement and auditing laws.

Article continues after this 

The provincial government recognized that as taxpayers and citizens of Zamboanga del Sur, “we all have the right to scrutinize our leaders. However, this right must be exercised responsibly, using verified facts and official documents.”

“Misrepresentation of audit findings not only misleads the public, but also undermines the integrity of democratic discourse,” the statement read.

Article continues after this 

Saniel warned that the Provincial Legal Office is prepared to pursue appropriate legal remedies against individuals or groups responsible for spreading the “distorted narrative.” /apl

World.title: Let NBI chief ‘speak his truth’ on VP Duterte’s threats vs Marcos – Ridon
World.content:
NBI Director Melvin Matibag —File photo by Mary Joy Salcedo | INQUIRER.net

MANILA, Philippines — Director Melvin Matibag of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) should give the full findings of the probe into Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. when he testifies during her impeachment trial on Tuesday — regardless of what issues senator-judges may raise.

“We don’t know what will happen when Director Matibag takes the stand. But, of course, our focus is to let him speak his truth, particularly on the whole comprehensive investigation that the NBI did,” Rep. Terry Ridon said in a mix of Filipino and English during the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City.

That was Ridon’s reply to a question on whether senator-judges could raise objections or matters unrelated to the impeachment case when Matibag testifies before the Senate impeachment court.

Article continues after this 

The impeachment article stems from Duterte’s Nov. 23, 2024 online press conference, during which she said she had instructed someone to kill President Marcos, his wife Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez — if she herself were killed.

The NBI investigated the remarks and recommended the filing of criminal charges for grave threats and inciting to sedition.

Full results of NBI probe

According to Ridon, Matibag is expected to present the result of the NBI’s overall investigation into Duterte’s remarks, including whether authorities found indications that the alleged threats against the president and his family remain ongoing.

“Basically, he’s giving the full report on the NBI investigation into the threats made by the vice president and whether there exist continuing threats by the vice president on the president and his family,” Ridon said.

The impeachment court has so far heard only from the NBI’s Cybercrime Division through the testimonies of Senior Agent John Mark Calilung and NBI Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc.

Article continues after this 

He said Matibag would provide a broader account of the investigation by discussing the work of other NBI offices that participated in the probe.

Explosive testimony?

Asked about what he had earlier described as a potentially explosive testimony, Ridon declined to elaborate.

Article continues after this 

“If I tell you that now, it won’t be explosive anymore. So let’s just wait for the testimony of Director Matibag,” he said.

Ridon said the prosecution would leave it to the senator-judges to decide whether to take up issues outside the impeachment complaint during Matibag’s appearance.

“As to what the senator-judges would do on extraneous matters not related to the impeachment, we leave it to them. After all, they also have the right to raise various issues here in our hearing,” he said.

Matibag is expected to be the prosecution’s final witness on the impeachment article accusing Duterte of grave threats, culpable violation of the Constitution, and betrayal of public trust.
