World.title: Australians love Bali, Thailand and Vietnam. Why do we ignore this gem?
World.content:
InspirationMalaysia Australians love Bali, Thailand and Vietnam. Why do we ignore this gem? James Manning July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians love Asia, and rightly so. From Bali to Bangkok and Hokkaido to Hanoi, there is an abundance of fantastic food and culture in our corner of the world. But one tropical paradise that is practically on our doorstep is often overlooked. Why do we ignore Malaysia? In the 12 months up to May this year, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Australians took roughly twice as many trips to Thailand and Vietnam, and five times as many trips to Indonesia, as they did to Malaysia. Whether you’re in the market for a well-earned rest from the chaos of modern life – think White Lotus vibes without breaking the bank – or a short stopover in Kuala Lumpur on the way to Europe, this country has a lot to offer. Here’s how to make it work for you. Tanjong Jara Resort by YTL Hotels on the east coast of Malaysia. The beach resort



From KL, take a one-hour flight to Kuala Terengganu on the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia. There’s no shortage of budget accommodation around the city, but my destination is a boutique resort about an hour south, near Kuala Dungun. 



If you’re game, you can even go snorkelling or scuba diving with whale sharks off the nearby Tenggol island (September is the best time of year to spot them). For something more passive, you can watch fireflies dance in the dark on an evening cruise up the Dungun River, just be sure to wear plenty of insect repellent and avoid wearing black (it attracts mosquitoes). For something more hands-on, visit the on-site turtle hatchery, which has rescued and relocated more than 100,000 eggs from potential poachers since 2016 (the eggs are still hunted and sold on the black market despite scientists debunking the myth that eating them can cure asthma). The numbers sound immense, but only one in 1000 hatchlings makes it to adulthood in the wild. As well as being hunted by reef sharks, ghost crabs, monitor lizards, and seabirds, juvenile turtles have to contend with ocean plastic and fishing trawler nets. This means as few as 100 adults may have survived as a result of this program, showing why many species remain critically endangered and highlighting the importance of the work. If you’re staying at the resort during nesting or hatching season (April through October) you can even opt in to receive a call in the middle of the night to help out. The rooms are superb, but it’s hard to stay indoors when the surrounding nature is so beautiful.



If not, you can laze by one of the two pools or enjoy a variety of treatments at the spa. I opt for the traditional Malay, which begins with a floral bath followed by a deep tissue massage with herbal oils, ginger and galangal to improve blood circulation. Beforehand, a form asks me if I want to leave energised, relaxed, stress-free, headache-free or with clearer skin. There is no “all of the above” option, but I tick every box nonetheless. I needn’t have worried, the masseuse, Aida, is a master with her hands. The next day I visit the nearby Dungun Market – home to endless stalls of fresh seafood, satay jellyfish, dried chillies, pickled lychees, and more herbs than I ever knew existed – before returning to the resort for a cooking class. We learn how to make the perfect beef rendang and coconut curry with prawns (tofu is available for vegetarians). The secret, it turns out, is palm sugar, also known as “Malaysian candy”. Traditional Malay-inspired lobby area at Tanjong Jara Resort. The food here, whether cooked by yourself or the staff, is a highlight. “People come here to heal and eat well,” says chef Ann, a larger-than-life character who has been working here for more than 20 years.



The sambal chilli sauce at the breakfast buffet is one of the best I’ve ever tasted. The only thing more addictive is the endless warmth and hospitality of the staff, all of whom seem genuinely happy to help guests with anything and everything. “My job is half job and half holiday,” says rooms manager Jazz Jusoh, only half-jokingly. Before checking out, more than once I seriously consider applying for a job and staying. The iconic twin spires of Kuala Lumpur’s Petronas Towers. iStock The city break If you’re in need of a pit stop on the way to Europe, Kuala Lumpur has a lot to offer, especially if you’ve already done Singapore and Hong Kong. “KL never sleeps,” a local cheerily informs me soon after I arrive, and many here seem to follow that maxim to a tee. You can shop ’til you drop at Pavilion or Suria mall, before checking out the view upstairs from the top of the Petronas Twin Towers (the world’s tallest building from 1996 to 2004).



For a more unique cultural experience (one with shops you won’t find in every other world city), check out the stalls at Central Market and the nearby Petaling Street Market. Or get out of the city on a day trip to visit the world-famous Batu Caves. At dinner time, head down to the Jalan Alor night market for freshly made nasi lemak, rendang, laksa, and – if you’re brave enough – durian. It’s not for me, but you do you. Lavantha cocktail bar in Kuala Lumpur. My night ends at Lavantha cocktail bar, an offshoot of the award-winning Penrose. Housed underground in what was previously a bank vault, it’s run by three friends, one of whom studied in Melbourne. The menu is full of modern twists on classics, and I opt for the blueberry Gibson, which adds blueberries, thyme and white balsamic vinegar to gin with refreshing results. It goes down well with the small plates on offer, including potato terrine with a miso yuzu emulsion and smoked salmon aguachile. Someone suggests kicking on to the nightclub Over and Above (apparently the place to be seen) but unlike KL, I do need to sleep and I call it a night. An island adventure on the west coast beckons.



Sea villas at Pangkor Laut Resort, off the west coast of Malaysia. The private island There are a lot more Malaysian islands beyond Penang and Langkawi. In fact, there are more than 800. So if it’s island living you crave, head north from KL up the west coast for about three hours to the state of Perak. From here, you can transfer to a private oasis. To arrive on Pangkor Laut by speedboat is to get a glimpse of how the other half live. There are 140 villas spread across this 120-hectare island, 43 of which are on stilts over water. There are two pools to choose from, but the best place to relax here is the spa village, a title it definitely earns – the place is enormous. Treatments start with a Chinese-style foot massage before men and women are separated for a three-part bathing experience.



The bath house at Pangkor Laut’s spa village. First up is a refreshing cold water pool, where you can be gently massaged by a series of waterfalls before unwinding in a hot Japanese-style onsen with a cup of ice-cold green tea. Finally, a full-body exfoliation before being led to a private villa for a 90-minute campur-campur treatment, which mixes traditional Malay and Thai massage. Every part of it is blissful, and I’d return to the spa every day if time and money allowed. If you feel inspired to continue your wellness journey, yoga classes are held in the mornings by the sea in a villa that also hosts operas once a year, inspired by a former guest, Italian tenor Luciano Pavarotti. Related Article Asia Asia’s 25 greatest cities to visit, ranked and rated Later, I catch a buggy to the private beach, and I’m nursing a cocktail while lazing in a hammock outside Chapman’s Bar. It’s named after British Colonel Freddy Chapman, who hid on the island from the Japanese during World War II before making a daring escape by swimming out to a British submarine.



Unlike competitors in the annual Chapman’s Challenge, I don’t attempt to recreate this feat, but I do indulge in a dip. The water is warm here (though not quite the perfection I enjoyed on the east coast). Plastic pollution is a problem due to recent storms so men with rakes and wheelbarrows do what they can. It’s like having your own private beach at Pangkor Laut Resort. It’s not the only environmental effort on this island, where endangered hornbills and flying foxes thrive. The conservation team also rehabilitate turtles that have swallowed plastic and can no longer dive to get food because they are too buoyant. There are even critically endangered pangolins here, although they’re incredibly rare. We don’t spot any, and I can’t help but feel the less human contact they have, the better. There are already long-tailed macaques on this island, and next year there are plans afoot to reintroduce another primate, the slow loris. “People say it’s futile but you have to try,” says the resort’s resident naturalist Aris. “I want to leave something for my kids.”

World.title: The rise and fall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime The rise and fall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family Riley Walter July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For gangland police, years of work had been leading to one day; they had intercepted phone calls, listened to conversations, surveilled targets and slowly but surely built briefs of evidence on Sydney’s underworld powerbrokers. In the early hours of a Wednesday morning, a little over two years ago, they moved in – 250 officers across the city’s south-west pounced in one of the most significant operations carried out by anti-gang police. Their targets – alleged senior members of the Alameddine organised crime network. By then, many of its highest-ranking members, including patriarch Rafat Alameddine, had fled the country for the safety of the Middle East. Left behind was a criminal syndicate estimated to be making $1 million a week from a sprawling drug trafficking empire. As the Alameddine family’s grip on the city’s lucrative drug trade increased, so too did the efforts of detectives on its tail. Finally, after years of pursuing the network’s upper echelons, they had broken through. The Alameddine organised crime network remains in Sydney in name only, police say. Aresna Villanueva



Having rounded up 16 people, including the family’s alleged local leader, Ali Elmoubayed, the message was clear: the Alameddine network’s Australian operations were all but finished, the infamous group had been eradicated, NSW Police Deputy Commissioner Dave Hudson said in March 2024. To the network’s puppet-masters abroad, the arrests signalled authorities’ focus despite their relocation. To the Alameddines’ underworld rivals, it signalled a shift in Sydney’s criminal landscape; no longer did the Merrylands clan rule the roost. The city was up for grabs. So swift has the downfall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family been since that senior police regard the Alameddine network as remaining in name only. As its once-feared enforcers have fled, been jailed or killed, its long-held grasp of the city’s illicit drug market has weakened. With a lack of local leadership, the struggle for a seat atop Sydney’s underworld has become a free-for-all; even the family’s most loyal followers have abandoned their allegiances to cash in on the city’s insatiable appetite for cocaine and methamphetamine. Members of KVT – a street gang comprising predominantly men of Fijian descent and long used by the Alameddine network as muscle – cut ties with their one-time allies during a mass exodus of powerbrokers from the crime family. Now, up against a contingent of turncoats and underworld upstarts, remaining members of the Alameddine network have become a hunted species. Rafat Alameddine, pictured in 2019, left Australia amid increased police scrutiny. Kate Geraghty



In January, the self-proclaimed Coconut Cartel firebombed the western Sydney home of Rafat Alameddine’s cousin, Bilal Alameddine. The cartel, comprising defected Alameddine network members and others vying for control of Sydney’s underbelly, vowed to “chalk out” any loyalists still flying the family’s flag; a line was drawn in the sand and war declared. The attacks since have been unrelenting and unwavering. In April, Rafat Alameddine’s vacant Merrylands home was peppered with bullets in a drive-by shooting, while homes and businesses linked to his brother-in-law, Asaad Alahmad, were targeted. Alahmad has been jailed for his involvement in Ready 4 War, the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation. The Coconut Cartel, which has rebranded several times in the past year, has claimed responsibility for the attacks under several gang names spruiked to gain notoriety. One, the so-called “Lone Wolves”, took the credit for several incidents in Sydney targeting the Alameddine network’s offshore leadership. The group, through video of their attacks and communications shared with burgeoning social media channel SCN Worldstar, promised an ever-increasing assault on the network. Day by day, the group said after claiming credit for an arson attack in April, it would drive the Alameddine network out of Sydney with the help of insiders willing to share the syndicate’s secrets. Another group believed to comprise alleged Coconut Cartel associates and members – dubbed the OC Jail Gang – also pledged its support to “eradicate” the Alameddines.





Closer to home, one of the last remaining alleged high-profile members of the network left on Sydney’s streets, the rapper “Ay Huncho”, recently heeded years of police warnings and left NSW after several threats to his life, including what detectives say was a foiled attempt to assassinate him in April. After a group of masked men allegedly kidnapped and beat his bodyguard in a late-night ambush, the rapper, whose legal name is Ali Younes, finally made himself scarce, relocating interstate. In May, Elmoubayed’s home was peppered with bullets as the 33-year-old languishes in custody, having been charged in December with plotting to murder a former ally, whose defection from the Alameddine network was the catalyst for months of tit-for-tat shootings and assassination attempts. Whatever their title, the groups targeting the Alameddine network have a common goal: seizing control of the underworld from its long-time rulers. “What we’re seeing now involves competing groups, shifting alliances and external actors trying to assert control,” Cook says. “These are loose, opportunistic networks with no hierarchy, no discipline and no long‑term loyalty. That lack of structure is one of the reasons conflicts escalate so quickly.” For police investigating the increased targeting of the Alameddine network, the blurred lines of the family’s rivals and the shifting criminal landscape present an increasingly challenging task; in a world where loyalty was a criminal’s most valuable asset, it is now a tradeable commodity. “The reality is that contract criminals move between groups, sometimes working for both sides of a conflict,” Cook says.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Drug kingpin’s suspected links to Vietnam assassination of Sydney cartel leader Recent drug seizures indicate South-East Asian organised crime groups have all but taken control of Sydney’s underworld from the Alameddine family. Overseas-based alleged kingpins, including former Sydney man Daniel Rodney Badger, have become the focus of detectives investigating the flow of drugs into Australia as criminal organisations band together to control the manufacture and supply of cocaine, methamphetamine and heroin. “When we dismantle one group, others step in to take the work and then we target them,” Cook says. “It’s a cycle we’re very familiar with.” Despite the distance between those police believe are pulling the strings abroad and the violence on Sydney’s streets, apprehending overseas-based organised crime figures is one of NSW Police’s highest priorities. “They hide behind foreign jurisdictions and encrypted platforms, but they are not out of reach,” Cook says. “When opportunities arise, we act. It may take time, but we don’t lose sight of them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: People think my suburb is posh, but it’s friendly and diverse – and I got my unit cheap
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion People think my suburb is posh, but it’s friendly and diverse – and I got my unit cheap Kellie Williams Contributor July 20, 2026 — 5:00am

July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When someone asks where I live and I say Ascot, the standard response is: “Ooh, fancy!” Yet I’m not rich, and I’ve never encountered snobbery here. Indeed, I’ve been regularly impressed by local shop owners who remember you by name from the first time you chat to them I have neighbours who are friendly and caring, not in an intrusive way, but genuinely look out for each other – like texting if I’ve accidentally left my garage door open, or picking up a package that’s been left in a weird spot by a delivery guy. On one occasion when I was sick, they’ve even offered to pick up groceries. There’s really no such thing as a typical Ascot person, just like there’s no such thing as a typical style of home in Ascot.



You know the place: that hilly suburb, landlocked by Albion, Clayfield, Hamilton and Hendra, a stone’s throw from the Brisbane River, the river you can easily see from so many vantage points in Ascot, from the hilltops to Kingsford Smith Drive. Named, obviously, after Ascot in England, hub of thoroughbred racing, our Ascot has long been a place for the betting on the nags, with Doomben and Eagle Farm Racecourse both taking up real estate here (and Albion Park just over the border). Ascot also has exceptional heritage houses such as Nyrambla, built in 1885. This one is especially interesting. It was requisitioned by the Allies in 1942 as a top-secret facility and used as a US-Australian intelligence base for codebreakers for three years – a Brisbane Bletchley Park. In the years since there have been several famous inhabitants, including ABC presenter Blair Edmonds, markets operator Jan Power, and beloved Queensland actor Bille Brown. As well as mansions, Ascot has art deco apartment buildings, Queenslander houses both updated and unrenovated, and daggy, rectangular unit blocks built between the 1960s and 1990s, giving it a very mixed aesthetic. There are big parks with towering trees, and local retail gems, such as the super-convenient IGA Marketplace at Oriel Park and the RSPCA Op Shop, full of quality finds, plus a variety of restaurants and cafes.



Inhabitants benefit from close access to great neighbours: Hamilton’s Eat Street Northshore, New Farm’s Powerhouse and James Street precinct, Newstead’s Bunnings, the Valley’s Homemaker, Albion’s Fonzie Abbott, Thai Ways and Bathhouse, and Clayfield’s convenient shops along Sandgate Road. We are also close to the airport, but I’ve never once heard a plane fly over. I’m a Sydneysider who lived in Cairns for a decade before moving to Brisbane in 2017. I had been renting across the inner south, inner east and inner west of Brisbane for six years when, as a middle-aged empty-nester happily enjoying my career and social life, I decided Brisbane was the best city in Australia to live in permanently, and was ready to purchase a property. Art deco apartment blocks on Lapraik Street. Markus Lavik This personal decision coincided with Brisbane’s COVID-induced property boom, and I was seeing prices increase steeply and steadily over the six months I was hunting. I was looking in the lower end of Brisbane’s price range, but wanted to be within a five-kilometre radius of the city. My biggest wishlist item was a private courtyard for my dogs and plants. To my surprise I just happened to find that in an Ascot unit. It was the second-cheapest one-bedroom unit I could find for sale in Brisbane when I bought it in mid-2023, and though it’s doubled in value in three years, it’s still one of the cheapest properties, and a very good investment. For that, I am grateful.



Though I moved to Ascot for the entry price and leafy courtyard, I quickly realised how lucky I was to live in such a pleasant and convenient suburb where it takes me no more than 15 minutes to get to the airport, the Valley, the city, two major hospitals, Westfield Chermside and even South Brisbane areas where I spend a lot of time socially. Related Article Public Transport We spent the morning at Brisbane’s loneliest train station Despite my preference for living close to town, I value having green spaces and nature close by. In my courtyard and neighbouring yards, I see owls, possums, lizards, pythons, bush turkeys and other birds, and did I mention lots of big trees? If I’m seeking an even quieter reprieve, just 20 minutes up the freeway I can relax at Sandgate and Brighton’s beautiful foreshore strips. Are we posh? Maybe some of the local schools are, and whoever’s living inside those grand mansions. But we’re a diverse suburb, with a warm, welcoming and safe community vibe.

World.title: Can NZ First pull off the 'drill baby drill' moment it dreams of?
World.content:
Winston Peters announces oil and gas exploration policy Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Analysis - New Zealand First, led by Parliament's longest serving MP, is playing the long game - both in building party support and policy.

Shane Jones' "drill baby drill" moment is "potentially" on its way, but can the party pull it off?

At the New Zealand First convention over the weekend, leader Winston Peters announced a plan to invest a billion dollars into surveying what oil and gas supplies could be extracted from the country's offshore basins.

Peters says it's a "game changer" and could lead to a fuel secure and resilient New Zealand, that also pays dividends. Just how much? That's not clear yet.

And when exactly would it happen? Potentially "within six years" - plenty of time for more wars and changes in government.

Labour doesn't support the idea and National won't give it a firm tick, only saying the party already supports oil and gas exploration, which means it's unclear it will get over the line exactly as it stands.

That doesn't bother Peters though, who said "what we're trying to do is change the political dichotomy to understand the potential".

Or, as the party said multiple times over the weekend, challenge the status quo - Pepsi versus Coke as Peters delighted in saying.

That, of course, is what minor parties can get away with - Peters criticised National and Labour for only tinkering with the fuel security issue by offering solar panel solutions.

It seems to be working better than most for New Zealand First, which is gaining support in all the polls.

History would tell us minor parties tend to be punished after being in government - New Zealand First is defying that.

What's more, it's eating into support from other parties, even gobbling up former politicians from both major parties.

There were all the greatest hits you might expect from a New Zealand First event, including a rallying call against Indian immigration, even as people of Indian descent were working at the event, topping up the food and clearing the plates.

Also - a request from a member for songs playing during the breaks to only play New Zealand music.

But there was also a sense that something had shifted, perhaps evidenced by the greatest number of delegates present at a conference in the party's history, many telling RNZ with a gleeful honesty they'd ditched other political parties to be there.

The event on Sunday. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

One member told RNZ that in previous years, they'd whispered about the fact they'd left other political parties for New Zealand First. This year, it was on full display.

"Grandad was blue, dad was blue, I was blue until I woke up," one new supporter told RNZ.

There was no irony in his voice at the mention of waking up, despite supporting "Winston's war against woke".

Here, too, Peters is playing the long game, lending his ear to those who don't quite fit in the "system".

One member - a mum from the East Coast - said she was there that weekend for the vaccine injured and a desire to maintain family and Christian values.

Her teenage daughter travelling with her said she felt the party was also about the next generation, despite being associated with people "older than me", she said.

Another member told RNZ her voice hadn't been heard during interactions with a medical practitioner.

Former National MP Harete Hipanga-Brownlie, now a New Zealand First candidate, said it out loud when describing the Parliament occupation protesting Covid-19 mandates.

"I saw thousands of New Zealanders gathered from all walks of life, I also saw Winston Peters walking amongst them."

The religious connotations were obvious, as the party also picks up socially conservative voters, but it was also a clear line drawn back in 2022, when New Zealand First wasn't even in Parliament.

Now, that support has clearly grown beyond just those railing against Covid-19 mandates that no longer exist, and a "globalist agenda".

It's the economy, stupid, or - as Peters said - "it's about the economy" and the "blue-collared worker".

The cost of power. The cost of grocery bills. The people doing it tough.

All parties know this election will be another cost-of-living election, but no party is cutting through on the issue quite like New Zealand First.

Tim, a solo dad who had driven from Wellington with his seven-year-old son for the convention, told RNZ it's the people that build the economy, but there was a sense from him that people in New Zealand were missing out, and priorities weren't in the right order.

Peters clearly has a way with the people, he's even quite happy to sit at the back of the room while the convention took place, on a raised platform for cameras, rather than a real seat.

He also has a way of convincing outcasts that New Zealand First will look after them.

His opponents from other parties would say he can't be trusted - but those who have parted ways with, or been sacked by, those parties have come to him in droves.

"I didn't leave Labour, Labour left me," said Stuart Nash at the convention, ignoring that he was sacked, but adding that Labour doesn't represent "hardworking Kiwis" anymore.

National's problem is "they've forgotten who they are" said former National MP Michael Laws, a "centre party doesn't stand for anything".

During his first speech of the weekend, Peters gave a nod to the age of New Zealand First, "seconds out of the ring for round 33".

That's a lot of rounds in a boxing match, and support has come and gone for Peters over that time. He knows exactly what it feels like to be chucked out.

He's said repeatedly now New Zealand First will turn the polls into confetti, that the party has far more support than what is being reported.

It seems at least some of that support is coming from National, and it makes it tricky for Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who is increasingly scathing in his assessment of New Zealand First's comments about the Indian free trade agreement.

But currently, Luxon's only way back to power is with his coalition partners, one of whom - New Zealand First - made the suggestion other parties should take off their knee pads when foreign leaders visit.

World.title: NZ First's $1b pledge for oil and gas exploration better spent on renewables - Greenpeace
World.content:
Winston Peters announces oil and gas exploration policy Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A climate activist says New Zealand First's billion-dollar pledge for oil and gas exploration would be better spent on investing in renewables.

New Zealand First announced at the weekend it would explore deep sea basins around the country for oil and gas if elected, saying that would shore up the country's fuel security.

The party would invest an initial $1b into a national survey fund.

Greenpeace chief executive Russel Norman said that money should instead be spent on investing in renewable electricity generation.

"That would actually give us energy sovereignty. It would mean cheaper energy and it would mean energy which doesn't destroy the climate."

New Zealand had a "great opportunity for energy sovereignty" by investing more in renewables, Norman said.

The billion-dollar fund was a gamble, and wouldn't guarantee power prices coming down, he said.

"It's a billion dollars you'd give to oil companies in the gamble that they might find something which might then be available in a decade's time, and then would destablise the climate."

Demand for oil and gas in New Zealand and worldwide was dropping, he said.

"We've already seen it massively in China, with the electrification of transport. We're just starting to see it here."

Winston Peters speaks at New Zealand First's campaign launch on Sunday. RNZ / Lillian Hanly

At New Zealand First's campaign launch on Sunday, leader Winston Peters said one of the most concerning issues facing the nation was fuel security and supply.

Peters said New Zealand potentially held Norway-scale energy prospects which had never been properly surveyed.

"If we identify those reserves in our basins, we will have the ability to utilise the natural resources we have to make our country secure, prosperous and to build real resilience."

He said within six years, the country could have a pathway to own and control its own supply of energy.

The party would place a royalty above 50 percent on all extractions as production matured.

National energy spokesperson Simeon Brown said the policy was a reminder that Winston Peters and Shane Jones supported a ban on oil and gas when in government with Jacinda Ardern.

World.title: 'Simplistic' colour-coded school reports get mixed reviews from principals
World.content:
Colour-coded ERO reports fail to ease principals' fears Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The publication of the first Education Review Office reports using colour-coded tables to depict schools' performance has done little to allay principals' fears.

The tables use four colours to show how schools are going in 14 areas, including attendance, reading and writing and teaching.

The colours show if schools are judged to be excelling (dark green), doing well (light green), working towards (orange) or improvement required (red).

Some principals worry the tables are too simplistic and will unfairly stigmatise schools in poor communities, where achievement and attendance is often lower than average.

The Education Review Office acknowledged the concern, and told RNZ it was particularly important people read the full reports of schools in poor communities and not base judgements just on the tables.

Westlake Girls' High School was among the first schools to receive one of the new reports.

Its table was mostly dark-green squares, with some light green and one orange, meaning the school was 'excelling' in most areas, 'doing well' in others and 'working towards' in just one area - attendance.

Principal Jane Stanley said it provided a better overall picture of the school's performance than previous reports - but only if people read the full document.

"It's certainly much more comprehensive than the previous ones were, and I think gives a really good picture of the school and what's going well, and things that might need to be added to or improved," she said.

Stanley said many parents would likely only read as far as the table.

"It's a really short summary of the work behind the full report," she said. "Unfortunately, people will probably go to that, and be drawn to that and not read behind."

Beaconsfield School, near Timaru, also received one of the new reports. Its table was mostly light-green squares, plus some dark green and two orange - for attendance and school governance.

Principal Hamish Brown says the table said a lot, but it did not tell the full story.

"The boxes are OK," he said. "They've indicated what they've found, but there's two steps behind those boxes and we feel that anybody reading it is not going to go deeper into the report."

For example, he said Beaconsfield received an orange rating for governance, because the school board had three new members, not because of any particular problem.

As for attendance, Brown said, with 120 pupils, a small number of children could have a big effect on the school's percentages.

Brown said he knew other schools were apprehensive about the new reports.

"There is a bit of nervousness simply because it is very black and white, and sometimes communities, local people papers, local media like to grab the short story without getting the full story," he said.

Principals Federation president Jason Miles. Supplied / NZPF

Principals Federation president Jason Miles said the tables were confronting and could be misleading, if people didn't read the rest of the report.

"It is very easy for someone to look at those colour ratings, without reading the details behind it to get a certain impression of some schools," he said.

He said the federation worried the attendance rating in particular was more a reflection of a school's socio-economic status than how good the school was.

"A school that may have had 40 percent attendance and worked really hard to increase it to 60 percent, but will still be marked in the 'working towards' area, rather than be rated on the hard work and support that they've put in to raising that attendance," he said.

The Education Review Office understood the concern that some people may look only at the colour-coded snapshot.

"The snapshot is only one part of the report," it said. "It is designed to help parents and whānau navigate the report, not replace the full report."

ERO said reading the full report was particularly important for schools serving communities with high levels of need.

"Where a school is making strong progress from a low base, or where teaching and leadership are effective, that will be recognised in the report," it said. "Each judgement is supported by narrative commentary explaining what the school is doing well, where improvement is needed and what actions will support better outcomes for learners."

It said the purpose of the reports was to support school improvement, and the changes were aimed at making reports clearer, more accessible and easier for parents, whānau, schools and boards to use.

"We will continue to listen to feedback from schools, parents and whānau as the new reports are used, so that our reporting remains clear, useful and centred on learners," it said.

World.title: Auckland Council ponders ways to increase voter turnout at 2028 elections
World.content:
Low voter turnout prompts election booth proposal Morning Report Download MP3 3m

In a bid to turn around its most dismal voter turnout since its establishment in 2010, Auckland Council is considering the introduction of general election-style polling booths.

Just 29 percent of Aucklanders voted in its local elections last year, prompting council officials to ask why.

A recent Auckland Council report said its staff believed changing the voting method alone was unlikely to reverse the trend of low participation.

In September, Auckland councillors will vote on whether to keep postal voting or introduce in-person booth voting for its 2028 elections, or a combination of both.

The council report estimated an IT-supported booth election over 10 days would cost between $39-55 million, tens of millions more than a postal election.

Sticking with the status quo of postal voting was projected to cost $15.5 million in 2028, up from $10.5 million in 2025, largely due to NZ Post increasing its rates.

The council said it was "exploring opportunities to reduce costs", including using council-owned venues, "procurement efficiencies", and encouraging voters to vote early and "arrive vote-ready".

Auckland's local boards were being asked for their views on both options.

Franklin Local Board member Gary Holmes said he would not support either.

"Choosing between them is like being asked whether you would rather drown slowly or freeze to death.

"Why would you spend tens of millions of dollars more to get the same outcome or worse?"

He wanted the council to push central government to allow it to implement online voting in 2028.

"Government has 27 months and no excuses."

He said the council already offered online voting for Business Improvement District programme ballots.

"If it's good enough for council to do it in one part of its game, we should be looking at it for local body elections."

In another report released this month by Local Government New Zealand, its Electoral Reform Working Group recommended running all local body elections as similarly as possible to parliamentary elections, including with booth voting.

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith, who was the chair of the working group, said councils should not be the ones deciding how their electors voted.

"I'm not that comfortable with councillors and mayors themselves making the decision about what form of voting is to be used in their area, because quite frankly, they have a direct conflict of interest.

"It's better made at arm's length and that's why one of our strong recommendations was that the electoral system for our councils be run independently by the Electoral Commission."

Victoria University of Wellington associate politics professor Lara Greaves said the rationale behind booth voting was to make the process easier and more enticing.

"There has been this long-running problem with local government turnout. It's declining and it's pretty low.

"One thing that people often propose is some kind of in-person voting booth. The idea is that you would have maybe a bit of a community feel, maybe a sausage sizzle, maybe a bouncy castle, whatever you could do to make a community feel and get people together in person.

"When we talk about voting booths, people normally think about those somewhere in people's environments, like maybe near a supermarket, or near a church or a school."

She said online voting came with increased security risks, which would be hard for companies contracted to run elections to manage.

"The problem with online elections is that people hack them. There's capacity for foreign interference or anything like that, so those systems have to be incredibly secure.

"The [election] providers would need to be able to re-assure the public, but also policymakers and central government, that these systems are secure and that's quite a big investment, especially if you're talking about companies."

She said people not knowing what local government did or enough about candidates also affected voter participation.

"People aren't necessarily paying attention to local government on a day-to-day basis. There aren't so many local papers anymore, local journalists, and they don't necessarily make that link between their everyday lives."

She said more needed to be done alongside exploring voting methods.

"When voter turnout hits the 20s and the 30s, it's starting to be a small minority of the public voting. I think that leads to questions as to what level of turnout these people elected no longer have a mandate?"

Auckland Council governance and engagement general manager Lou-Ann Ballentyne said the council's findings from the 2025 election showed public awareness was low.

She said, regardless of the voting method the council chose, its would do its best to promote the election.

She said legislative change allowing the council to consider online voting was unlikely to be in place for the 2028 local elections, but Auckland Council's submission to the parliamentary inquiry into last year's local elections supported revisiting it in the future.

A spokesperson for the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) said the government was not considering online voting for local elections, due to security concerns.

World.title: 'You've done magic on my feet': Trainee healthcare workers fight diabetes amputations
World.content:
Two Northland women have gone from struggling to find work to fighting the region's diabetes epidemic.

Christine Hape and Hineataahua Brown are training to become New Zealand's first "footcare assistants", working alongside podiatrists to help prevent amputations from diseases like diabetes.

Hape hadn't planned on working with feet when she moved to Northland.

"I'm loving it," she laughed. "I didn't realise how much I love feet.

"Why I love it is just seeing our whānau stand up and say, 'Oh my gosh, I feel like I'm walking on a cloud. Oh, you've done magic on my feet'. Tthat's pretty heartwarming for myself."

The former special-needs teacher was looking for caregiving work, when the Ngāti Hine Health Trust approached her with an unexpected opportunity.

The clinic is the first in the country to hire and train footcare assistants, a new qualification aimed at preventing diabetes-related amputations.

Chief executive Tamati Shepherd-Wipiiti says diabetes is massively over-represented in his region.

"Our patient database tells us that over 60 percent have either type 1, type 2 or are pre-diabetic," he said. "Now that's three times the national average.

"Diabetes is killing our whānau."

When the government announced the qualification last year, Shepherd-Wipiiti jumped at the chance to boost the clinic's diabetes workforce.

"We were first in the country to trial the new foot care assistant credential," he explained. "We took two wonderful wahine toa, who came off the benefit.

"We're putting them through their training, which involves online and work-based learning.

"They can become qualified footcare assistants in November and they'll be the first two in the country."

Hape said her role was to ease the burden on Ngāti Hine's podiatrist, who has seen enormous demand in recent years.

"We take care of all the basic footcare that helps lessen the load for our podiatrists - basic nail cutting, filing," she explained.

"At the moment, we specialise in doing the diabetic foot assessments for our whānau. We can then refer them on to our podiatrist."

Hape and colleague Brown travelled rural Northland to run outreach clinics and house visits for those who couldn't travel to Whangarei.

Brown grew up in Ngāti Hine, but said she never realised how widespread diabetes had become.

"Coming from Ngāti Hine, diabetes was never talked about. Before I started my role, I didn't know anything about diabetes," she said.

"I didn't even know my own grandfather had diabetes. I didn't know that my nana couldn't get to the doctors, so she wasn't going to her appointments.

"When we go out there, our nurses are able to give her those simple health checks and we're able to give them footcare, and everything they need is at their fingertips."

Balancing her work in the community with online classes to earn her certification, she said the last several months had fast-tracked her education.

"It's really cool to do theory, and then be able to - the next day - go and actually do the practical work," she said. "We're able to study statistics, and then we're going into the community and seeing them firsthand."

Brown felt the clinic was breaking the stigma around diabetes and patients were grateful.

"I've had a kuia that's tried to shove $100 down my scrub top," she laughed. "I am not lying.

"We've had kuia that stand up after our outreaches have finished and their voices are wiri-ing from gratefulness, because they were so embarrassed of their feet."

Shepherd-Wipiiti said his own complications from type 2 diabetes had shown him the importance of footcare.

"I have myself had a partial foot amputation," he said. "I lost the front of my left foot.

"I know what that means and I know what it means for whānau. I have a two-year-old daughter.

"I'm about to have a son, and I want to do basic things like run around and kick a ball, and I'm able to and I want other whānau to be able to."

World.title: National toll road plan held up even as government faces funding hole
World.content:
A national plan for introducing more tolls on roads and a strategy for using more tolling powers are running two years behind schedule.

This comes at a time when the government has had to slow down on building significant highways for lack of money.

Transport Agency Waka Kotahi admits it has been held up by "internal capacity constraints".

The plan and strategy first due last year will now not be out until the first half of next year.

The "strategic tolling position" would cover how the agency can deploy new tolling powers in legislation currently before parliament.

This position would be used "when considering new roads for tolling" and how that fits with paying for roads as a whole, NZTA told RNZ this week.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop last week revealed a slowdown in when some of the highways would be built, saying National's commitments in 2023 were "very ambitious" and circumstances had changed.

RNZ asked Bishop if his revised timeline took into account the information gap from not having done a tolling plan yet, but he did not respond.

"The minister doesn't have anything to add beyond NZTA's statements to you."

'Large volume' of work

The national tolls plan had been due in 2025, about the time the government began taking a new look at how to pay for the billions of dollars needed for the Roads of National Significance or RONS.

NZTA cited a logjam for the hold-up.

"Work on the strategic network assessment and the development of a national tolling plan was deferred from 2025 to 2026, primarily due to internal capacity constraints, resulting from the large volume of project-based tolling work that has been required in the past two years" then pushed out again to 2027, it said.

Last year, it said it was doing tolling assessments of a dozen or so RONS, including the Northland corridor to Whangārei, Mill Road in west Auckland and Tauriko West, near Tauranga.

Recently, it has worked up proposals for - and the government has agreed to - tolls on three new highways in the North Island - Ōtaki to north of Levin, Penlink in north Auckland and the Takitimu North Link from Tauranga to Te Puna.

Earlier, tolls were agreed for the 7km O Mahurangi Penlink stretch between Whangaparaoa Peninsula and State Highway One, north of Auckland, not now due to be completed until 2029. At first due in 2026, it has been delayed by slips and "challenging" construction conditions at Wēiti River Bridge, which will also push out its $830m cost.

Only three highways currently have tolls north of Auckland and around Tauranga.

New powers to toll

The delayed plan and strategy go hand-in-hand, and aim to give the new legislation traction.

In 2024, the government said all big new road projects must look at tolling, and it needed law changes to allow more ways and reasons to deploy tolls.

The Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill that passed its second reading under urgency in June would enable "corridor tolling" for the first time - where an existing (not a new) road can be tolled, if its users benefit from the construction of a new road in the same corridor.

Tolls can be politically fraught. National cabinet minister and Kaipara ki Mahurangi MP Chris Penk has posted online, telling voters he is pushing for better infrastructure, while emphasising drivers must retain the choice of a free road near any new toll road.

A report back on the bill by the select committee recommended specifying that motorists must get at least one of four benefits - saving time, higher safety, reliability or resilience.

It recommended removing "efficiency" as a benefit, saying that should be demonstrated through the benefits users get.

The law change would also expand what toll revenue can be used for, beyond just for the new highway concerned, and its debt repayments and operating costs. Tolls would be adjusted annually by the rate of Consumers Price Index inflation.

Where the toll goes

Another constraint on more use of tolls has been the old camera technology. The transport agency has now worked for years to overhaul it - RNZ is seeking more details of where that is up to.

The new "strategic tolling position" will operationalise 2024's policy statement around tolls, said the agency, "confirming how the additional powers contained in the... bill would be used".

"Within this, NZTA is considering the role of tolling in the broader transport system, such as its role in relation to other funding and financing tools, or network performance interventions.

The existing three tolls roads have fees between $2.10-2.60 for a car and $5.20-5.60 for a truck.

The Northern Gateway Toll Road, north of Auckland, had 8.6 million tolls paid on it in 2023-24, generating enough revenue over time to pay back debt and potentially move the toll by 2038.

At the Tauranga Eastern Link Toll Road had 4.1 million trips that year and might be toll free by 2037, and Takitimu Drive had five million and might be toll free by 2031.

From every $2.60 car toll, $1.46 goes towards debt repayment, 80c to operating costs of the toll systems and 34c to GST.

World.title: Struggle to hear at parties? You're not alone
World.content:
When I was 25, I thought I was losing my hearing. I could hear clearly in normal situations, but I struggled at parties and networking events where many people would be speaking at the same time.

After countless times standing in a circle with people laughing at a clearly very funny joke that I could not even hear, I took myself to get a hearing test.

There I was, prepared to be told that I need to live with a hearing aid for the rest of my life. But instead, I was told that my hearing was perfectly fine.

The good news was that I didn't need to worry about what colour I wanted for my hearing aid, the bad news was I continued to feel alone at parties.

But it turns out that it's not just me. I'm struggling with a well-researched issue: "The cocktail party effect."

Clara Zhang, PhD candidate at the University of Auckland's Faculty of Engineering and Design, has been looking into it.

"My research is on improving the perception of non-native speakers in noise. Cocktail party is a very typical noisy environment, and non-native listeners are typically more disadvantaged when they're listening in noise."

In research, cocktail party means a noisy setting where there could be a large quantity of people speaking at the same time, and there could be other environmental noises such as clinking of the glass, traffic and buzz from machines.

Zhang said the effect was first defined and named in the 1950s, and affects both native and non-native listeners.

She said noisy environments made it harder to isolate the speech from the background noise, even if it's being made by the person right in front of you.

Pouria Bahmani Kolour (right) organises language exchange events around Auckland. Pouria Bahmani Kolour / Supplied

It's easier for native listeners as their ears are sharper at distinguishing the sounds. But for non-native listeners like me who grew up speaking a different language, everything muddles into one big pot of boiling noise.

In the 2023 census, 24 percent of those living in New Zealand said they spoke a second language other than English or te reo Māori.

Pouria Bahmani Kolour, who organises language exchange events around Auckland, is also familiar with the problem.

"Many people, many immigrants have the same common problem. Some people actually get very frustrated. They blame themselves for not studying enough, not trying hard. Some people don't actually care, they just let it slide."

He said their events were set up afterhours in a quiet cafe, and hopefully prepared participants for noisier events in the future.

"We are trying to make a calm environment for the people who participate to be able to actually hear each other and speak."

Kolour's native language is Farsi and he's a strong believer in "practice makes perfect".

He said his listening had improved significantly since attending four language exchanges a week.

Zhang said while practicing the language helped, asking for help was also important.

"I think studies have shown that non-native listeners, even if you have a lot of experience and you are very proficient, you still can't quite reach the native behaviour, so I think maybe you want to ask the speaker to come a bit closer to you or ask them to speak slower."

She said organisers could also mitigate the effect, by choosing a venue with better acoustic settings, for example, using a larger space that allow groups to scatter.

Audiologist Angela Loucks Alexander said some treatment and training may also help.

Specialising in Auditory Processing Disorder, Dr Loucks Alexander said some native-listeners who were not experiencing hearing loss may also find themselves unable to hear clearly.

Audiologist Angela Loucks Alexander says trainings used to help those with Auditory Processing Disorder can also help non-native listeners in noisy settings. Angela Loucks Alexander / Supplied

"Auditory Processing Disorder is a hearing problem that has less to do with the ears and more to do with the brain, it's difficulties in understanding what you hear. People can go in and have a test done and find out that their hearing sensitivity is within normal limits, but they may have a hard time understanding what they hear."

She said five to 15 percent of the population had the disorder, which affects both children and adults, and could present more in some groups than others.

Alexander said while non-native listeners may not be suffering from the disorder, they could still benefit from the training that was used in the treatments.

"So auditory processing can be improved because the brain is plastic, and we can actually train the brain in how to hear better in noise. I just want people to know who have these difficulties that there is hope."

She said the number of professionals who could help with the disorder had been growing, and she had set up a map to help those to find the right help.

Currently, most treatments required private funding, but Alexander hoped that with more research and awareness, this could change.

"When they can't hear and understand, they don't feel heard and understood, and I think this is a huge problem here in New Zealand."

I'm not sure whether I will seek treatment yet.

But speaking with the experts does make me feel... heard.

World.title: Live: FIFA's first-ever half-time show pauses deadlocked Spain-Argentina final
World.content:
I am no pop music critic, just a humble sports reporter. But here's my hot take.

Based on crowd involvement and vibes, Shakira singing Dai Dai easily topped the rest.

The fans mostly stayed in their seats to watch the show without being overly excited.

Everyone was given their own colourful flag to wave for the final song which was nice for the visual effect.

It all felt really quick and somewhat underwhelming, not as spectacular as a Super Bowl half time performance.

I've said it before and I'll say it again, if you just had a tight 10 minute set from Bon Jovi playing all the hits I reckon that would've done the trick.

WHOOOOOOAAAAA WE'RE HALFWAY THERE ...

World.title: Antonelli extends F1 championship lead, heartbroken Russell crashes out in Belgium
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has extended his lead at the top of the F1 championship standings with victory in the Belgian Grand Prix, with George Russell crashing out in the first lap and Oscar Piastri overcoming an early knock to finish fifth.

Piastri suffered minor damage to his car in the incident which saw him collide with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, who was cleared of wrongdoing by race officials and went on to claim second place.

And Piastri, who won this race last year, recovered well to ensure he finished in the scoring places behind Antonelli, with Max Verstappen third behind Leclerc.

Lewis Hamilton was placed fourth, but his Ferrari team are under investigation for an unsafe release, so there could yet be a change of order.

The incident followed another early controversy when Russell was forced to retire on the first lap after a prang with fellow Briton Hamilton to deal a huge blow to the Mercedes man's title hopes.

Russell, who had started third on the grid was attempting to overtake Hamilton when his rear wheel was tagged by the Ferrari driver, sending him spinning into the gravel and forcing the arrival of the safety car.

Russell drops to third in the drivers' championship and was fuming with the outcome having lost further ground on title leader Antonelli, and was once again left baffled by a mystery engine issue causing a speed deficit.

"I just got totally swallowed up down the straight, I lost three positions down the straight, down into turn five, then the incident was a racing incident," Russell told the host broadcaster.

"Maybe I could have gone a bit wider, maybe he could've braked a bit more.

"The incident shouldn't have happened if I had the speed down the straight.

"Very, very disappointing … felt like I was in a position to fight for the lead after turn one and suddenly no power and it's all gone."

Russell was bitterly disappointed with his early exit from the race. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

The victory was the sixth of the season for teenage driver Antonelli and the first since last month's Monaco Grand Prix, which leaves him 45 points clear of Russell in the championship.

"Let's go!" he screamed to the Mercedes team over the radio.

"Thank you so much, guys, thank you."

Piastri's McLaren team-mate, Lando Norris, started 13th due to a grid penalty but he still finished seventh after a pit-stop delay.

Frenchman Isack Hadjar finished sixth behind Piastri for Red Bull, despite starting at the back of the field because of a penalty.

AAP/ABC

Relive all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Brondello suspended by WNBA for inappropriate comment
World.content:
Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been suspended for one game by the WNBA for an inappropriate comment she used during a Toronto Tempo game against the Atlanta Dream.

Brondello, who coaches the Tempo as well the Opals, will miss Tuesday's AEST game against the Las Vegas Aces.

"The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league," the league said in a statement announcing the suspension.

During the 111-92 loss to the Dream on Saturday AEST, the broadcast picked up Brondello addressing officials after Tempo player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury following contact with Angel Reese.

Sabally was called for the foul and Brondello could be heard saying Reese was a "protected species".

The "protected species" phrase is commonly used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player.

In the US, however, the phrase can be considered derogatory towards black people.

Angel Reese took to social media in response to Sandy Brondello's comment. (Getty Images: Mark Blinch)

Brondello posted an apology on social media.

"Angel, I'm sorry," Brondello wrote on X.

"Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara's injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you."

How Brondello hopes to topple US No country has been able to topple the United States at either the FIBA World Cup or the Olympics since 2006. Here's what Sandy Brondello is doing to try to get Australia's Opals over the hump.

Reese took to social media after the game, posting: "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" and tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

"I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for black women in our league, and I'm deeply sorry for that," Brondello posted.

"I've spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible black women."

Brondello added: "I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply.

"I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment."

World.title: Argentina fans stage Times Square takeover ahead of World Cup final
World.content:
Times Square is usually filled with street performers in various costumes, with Spider-Man, Mickey Mouse, Elmo, and others angling to draw tourists in for photos.

Ahead of the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, the crossroads of the world had probably its most popular lookalike ever, a Lionel Messi doppelganger who was swamped by his compatriots.

It was a staggering scene at one of the world's most iconic meeting points, which has hosted large fan celebrations throughout the tournament, but the scale of this one looked to eclipse them all.

This Lionel Messi doppelganger was the life of the party in Times Square. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Argentina's fans have hosted a "banderazo" or pre-game rally before all their games, and have been among the biggest and most lively celebrations of all supporter groups, while Spanish fans had their own celebrations around New York too.

This has been a World Cup with so much excellence on the pitch from the biggest names in men's football.

But one of the biggest highlights and lasting memories for many will be the way travelling fans, locals and diaspora communities have come together for a joyous shared experience.

Stay across the latest news, analysis and features from the 2026 FIFA World Cup here.

Fan frenzy

The Argentina celebration started in the early evening, and was still throbbing with what looked to be thousands of fans hours later.

Some of them were lucky enough to have tickets for the final, but many more flew to New York just to experience the atmosphere here ahead of the decider, including Nazarena, who is originally from Buenos Aires, but now lives in Atlanta.

Fans said they wanted to celebrate together in New York, even if they did not have tickets to the game. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

"It's my country; I'm living in the United States right now, I had to come here. The environment, my country, my people, look!"

Many fans had similar sentiments, riding on a euphoric wave.

"We are not good in economy, we are not good in many things but we have a big heart so let's go Argentina," one fan said.

The Argentine fans have been grabbing headlines for their huge banderazo through the US, but there is a strong Spanish presence in New York too.

Many Spanish fans have been watching games at La Nacional in Manhattan's West Village.

"I think the Argentines, wherever they go, they bring a lot of people, and the Spaniards don't always bring a lot of people, but the few people we do bring cheer a whole lot," Spain fan Emilio said.

"So, I think we're going to be able to handle the Argentines."

La Nacional, part of the Spanish Benevolent Society in Manhattan, has been a key gathering place for the community throughout the World Cup.

Founded in 1868, it is the oldest Spanish cultural institution in the US, holds community cultural events and runs a non-profit restaurant.

It is expecting hundreds of fans to gather there for the final, and many more to flock there for celebrations should Spain win.

Ania Lopez from La Nacional says the World Cup has brought the Spanish community in New York together. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

"The Spanish live football in a very passionate way," La Nacional's community manager Ania Lopez said.

"We've been very popular [during the World Cup], because we are a reference point for the Spaniards that are here.

"For this final, it's been crazy the amount of emails that we have. But we are proud to be part of this."

World.title: Tom Trbojevic gutted after another injury, Titans, Dolphins record wins
World.content:
The Dolphins recovered from the shock of their 66-0 thrashing in Round 19 to claim a dominant derby victory over the Cowboys that puts them up to fifth on the NRL ladder.

Earlier, the Gold Coast Titans overcame a shocking start to win a 38-32 shootout against Manly Warringah at Robina.

Manly got off to a flying start, with Tom Trboojevic scoring the opening try in the first minute.

However, he was forced to leave the field soon after with a hamstring injury, another hamstring issue after he missed eight weeks earlier this year.

Trbojevic slipped over trying to catch a Joey Walsh pass and walked off the field covering his face in disappointment.

"Hopefully [it's] not as bad as the last one, but naturally he's pretty disappointed," Sea Eagles coach Kieran Foran said.

"We'll wait until he gets a scan and then work out the damage."

The injury to his hamstring is the ninth he has recorded in the past eight seasons, this being the fifth he has suffered on his right side.

The injury that ruled him out earlier this season was on his left.

Isaako stars and Dolphins thrive at Lang Park

Jamayne Isaako scored a cracker of a try. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

In the second game, Jamayne Isaako scored two tries and kicked six out of six off the tee as the Dolphins powered past the Cowboys.

The Cowboys leaped into a 10-0 lead inside the opening minutes, with the returning Tom Dearden scoring a try and setting one up for Jeremiah Nanai on his return from an ankle injury that ruled him out through the Origin period.

However, once the Dolphins got going, thanks to a typically spectacular score by Isaako in the corner, they never looked back.

The Dolphins' sixth win in a row at Lang Park moves them to fifth on the NRL ladder.

In the NRLW, the Titans thrashed the Eels 50-12 and the Broncos beat Wests Tigers 40-12, while later, the Knights play the Dragons.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: Hinkley set to coach Devils, Caddy taken to hospital as Dons end drought
World.content:
Ken Hinkley is set to be unveiled as the inaugural coach of the Tasmania Devils as Essendon ended a 12-game losing streak despite losing star forward Nate Caddy.

Hinkley met with Devils officials in Hobart on Sunday, with an announcement set to be made on Monday morning.

His impending arrival in Tasmania is a blow to veteran coaches John Longmire and Nathan Buckley, who were both in the running for the role.

Caddy left the field in the first quarter of Essendon's upset 10.7 (67) to 8.16 (64) win over the GWS Giants at Docklands Stadium after experiencing an irregular heart beat.

He was taken to a nearby hospital soon after for further assessment.

Essendon's win was its first inside Victoria since May 23 last year when it defeated Richmond in the Dreamtime in the G clash.

Elsewhere on Sunday, the Western Bulldogs defeated Gold Coast 11.11 (77) to 9.14 (68) at Carrara Stadium, dealing the Suns their eighth consecutive loss.

In Sunday's first match, Hawthorn recorded a 18.14 (122) to 6.16 (52) win over Richmond at the MCG as Nick Watson kicked five goals on his return to the side.
